I have been on the sea for many days, and I just cannot get tired of it.

Being out at sea has provided me so much, and I think that every young boy should grow up to be a sea- faring cowboy.

The Seagoing Cowboys Program gives me a sturdy job, amazing adventures, and time with my friends who liven up even the dullest events.

A cow sounds its classic grunt as the ship rocks gently from side to side, which means it is time to start working.

Who wouldn't want to wake up like that?

I absoulutely love doing it!

When working on a boat with what seems like a million animals there are some rough tasks, but that makes it so much easier to develop new skills.

Every single day you must feed the large and small animals two or three times in twenty- four hours, with the same scheudle for drinking, push a couple of bales of hay or oats for them to nibble on, and clean the stall.

See, a sturdy job!

Or, you could delve into the life of a night watch man.

Which of course I am not the best at, which means there is plenty of room for someone who . . . is!

Although the jobs may sound hard, there is plenty of time to sit back and relax.

Greece, Venice, China:

all places you can go if you are signing up to be a Seagoing Cowboy.

As the wind pushes the boat across the ocean, it pushed us with it, so of course we could not just resist the exotic opportunities!

In Greece we marveled at the amazing Acropolis, in Venice we were paddled across streets of water as the cool air blew across our faces, and in China we were able to tour the towns of culture.

We also were able to vist Crete and the Panama Canal prior to arriving in China.

Now, these trips are like vacations; but they are actually free!

If you are a sea- faring cowboy, then you are able to work, get payed, and vacation around different and unique cultures.

Like I said earlier, friends who can liven up a boring event are also helpful when touring amazing places and staying on the cattle-boat.

If you become a Seagoing Cowboy, you never know what kind of people you will meet.

I have met so many amazing personalitites, this being my fourth trip.

When having free time in between work, some cowboys participate in the eventful volleyball, table- tennis, fencing, boxing, whittling, games, reading, and baseball helping the long trip be fun and full of joy.

Touring cities with friends makes you feel so amazing and happy, it would be a miracle if you did not fly right off the ground from your joyful state.

What an amazing journey, and one that every single on of you should particiapte in!

Are you thinking about becoming a Seagoing Cowboy?

If you are, that is exellent!

The time working in a stable job, clearing entire exotic cities, and enjoying time with friends are all a package if you accept this job.

So, if you are ready to take the career, I am ready to hand you a sea inspired cowboy hat!

For years people have been wondering if there is life outside of Earth. There has been many movies, stories, and television shows that try to illustrate how civilizations outside of Earth will be like. Although these forms of media are very interesting and are entertaining, they tend to give people crazy ideas in their heads. One example of how crazy people can get is what happened when a satellite took a picture of Mars that had a landmass that shared the likeness of a human face. Most smart people knew it was a coincidence, but crazy conspiratists believe it was made by aliens. When you check your facts, compare Face to actual landforms on Earth, and see the picture of the Face in the highest resolution the answer is clear. The Face is just a lifeform that just happens to look like a face.

First of all, before I start explaning the scientific reasons why the Face is just a natural lifeform, think critically. If there was an alien civilization on Earth, and there is other life, wouldn't it have been found by now? If there was an alien civilization, there probably would be more evidence lying around, not just one coincidentally shaped structure on Mars. Countless rovers, space telescopes, and cameras have been through Mars and other planets, yet nothing has been found that proves that aliens have been through there.

When you look at how the landform of the Face is shaped, it looks similiar to something commonly seen on Earth. It looks like a butte or a mesa, landforms that are commonly seen around the American West. The chief scientist for NASA's Mars Exploration Program, Jim Garvin, says that "It (The Face) reminds me most of Middle Butte in the Snake River Plain of Idaho... That's a lava dome that takes the form of an isolated mesa about the same height as the Face on Mars." Mesas are natural occuring. If they can occur naturally on Earth, they can occur naturally on Mars.

In April 8, 2001 on a clear summer day, the Mars Global Surveyor took a picture of the Face to once and for all prove that their are no alien markings on it. A picture was taken previously on 1998, but it was a cloudy day, and skeptics believed that the haze was hiding something. They used the Surveyor's highest resolution posible, which scanned 1.56 meters a pixel, compared to the 43 meters per pixel that the 1976 Viking photo that started it all took. When the picture was taken, it did not show anything suspicious, in fact it looked like "the Martian equivalent of a butte or mesa". The Face on Mars has been debated for over 25 years. Some think it was created by ancient aliens, proving that there was once, or still is, life on Mars. Although this is an interesting theory, there are many reasons that this is not possible.

In 1976, the Face on Mars was first captured on camera by the Viking 1 spacecraft. In the photo there appears to be the face of "an Egyptian Pharaoh" carved into the rock. At first glance the structure looks man-made. When NASA released the photo to the public, it said that it was a,"huge rock formation...which resembles a human head...formed by shadows giving the illusion of eyes, nose, and mouth." Notice that NASA said the illusion of facial features. The features were just caused by shadows.

In 1997, 18 years later, another picture of the Face was taken. NASA took this picture because they "felt that it was important to taxpayers," the article says. It also claims that,"Few scientists believed the Face was an alien artifact..." When the photo was taken, the" team snapped a picture ten times sharper than the original Viking photos." This allowed you to see that the places appearing to be eyes and a mouth were just large craters. Some claimed that it was during the cloudy season on Mars so the clouds were hiding alien made features. When looking at the picture however, you can clearly see natural crevices and formations in the rock.

On April 8, 2001, yet another picture was taken of the Face. This time, the best picture yet was taken on a "cloudless summer day in Cydonia." There were no wispy clouds blocking the Face from view and the camera was much better than the one used on the Viking.

Jim Garvin, the chief scientist for NASA's Mars exploration program, states that,"Malin's team captured an extraordinary photo using the camera's maximum resolution." The article aso claims that,"Each pixel in the 2001 image spans 1.56 meters, compared to 43 meters per pixel in the best 1976 Viking photo." In this photo there are clearly no clouds blocking the view and actual geographical features of the formation are revealed. Gavin says that,"It reminds me most of Middle Butte in the Snake River Plain of Idaho..."

In conclusion, the Face is just a natural formation. Many like it are present here on Earth. Yet while the Face on Mars might not be an alien artifact, it is still an amazing glimpse of what the universe has to offer and new discoveries that are just around the corner.

Whether or not this is true, the author does not support this claim very well. There are many holes in this argument that are relatively easy to spot.

The first issue with the article is that it doesn't explain all of the issues that could come with exploring Venus, specifically financial issues. Although the article does a good job of explaining why it may be difficult to explore Venus, it does not explain the financial concerns of exploring Venus. The article should be able to tell the reader how big NASA's budget really is, and also hypothetically how much money it would cost them to explore Venus. Without acknowledging the fiscal concerns of exploring Venus, the author has left a hole in his or her argument. The author likes to point out the different types of technology that NASA can create to explore Venus, but the author doesn't explaing how much of a dent this new technology would put into NASA's budget. A well written article would have laid out how much exploring Venus would cost, and then would have explained why the financial expenses are worth the cost. Instead, by not adressing the fiscal concerns of the exploration of Venus, the reader is left wondering what the true consequences of exploring Venus really are.

The second problem with this article is that it does not address what NASA would even do if and when they got there. No where in the article does it mention what we could do on Venus even if we were able to study Venus from up close. The article explains that NASA could get a "blimp-like vehicle" to hover around 30 miles above Venus and study it from a distance. However, in the very next paragraph the author dismisses this idea and explains why it is not a viable option. Then, in paragraph seven the author explains what we could use to explore Venus, but still fails to explain how exactly this could be acheived. If there is no viable reason to explore Venus, then there should be no motive to explore Venus. Instead of strengthening his or her flimsy argument, the author instead tries to simply tell the reader that it is an indisputable fact that there is value in exploring Venus. Without any evidence of exploring Venus being beneficial, the whole article crumbles. The claim that humanity should explore Venus despite the difficulties that come with it falls apart because there is no rational explanation for why exploration would help anyone in the first place.

The author makes the well-supported claim that, despite the dangers, the study and exploration of Venus is worth the risk.

The author makes several points to support his claim. First, the author points out that Venus is one of the closest planets to Earth, in addition to Mars. Because of the length of time required for space travel, it makes sense to focus on the planets closest to Earth. The less time it takes to travel to a destination, the more time can be spent there, researching and observing. Another point that the author makes is that Venus may have once been much more like Earth than it is now. A long time ago, Venus may have had oceans like ours, which could have supported life. Even today, Venus' geological features are very similar to Earth's--Venus has valleys, mountains, and craters, just like Earth does. Studying Venus could provide a deeper insight into the formation and geological history of our own planet. Finally, the author gives examples of how scientists are working on ways to overcome the harsh Venusian conditions long enough for meaningful observations to be made. Up that far, temperatures would still be hot (about 170 degrees Fahrenheit), but they would be managable, and the air pressure and radiation levels would be like that of Earth. Other innovations, such as making simple electronics with silicon carbide or mechanical computers without any of the delicacy of modern electronics, are also being developed. Altogether, the points that the author makes are enough to convince anyone that the exploration of Venus is a worthy pursuit.

"Often referred to as Earth's "twin," Venus is the closest planet to Earth in terms of density and size, and occasionally the closest in distance too." Meaning, Venus is simple to see in the night, but "a very challenging place to examine more closely."

Several humans have sent numerous spacecraft to land on Venus-- "each previous mission was unmanned, and for good reason, since no spacecraft survived the landing for more than a few hours." Many different spacecrafts were sent to Venus's surface and none survived. Venus's atmosphere is almost 97% carbon dioxide. The even more harder and challenging part: the clouds are made up of "highly corrosive sulfuric acid." Venus's surface temperature "averages over 800 degrees Fahrenheit, and the atmosheric pressure is 90 times greater than on Earth." Also, "Venus has the hottest temperature of any planet in our solar system." There are also supposedly impediments like erupting volcanoes, powerful earthquakes, and frequent lightning strikes to probes seeking to land on its surface."

"Astronomers are fascinated by Venus because it may well once have been the most Earth-like planet in our solar system." Scientists believe that Venus long ago had oceans and various, different forms of life. The scientists also want to study/visit Venus more because it has some of the same features that Earth has like: "surface of rocky sediment and includes familiar features such as valleys, mountains, and craters." NASA has a solution of how to get people to Venus. "NASA's possible solution to the hostile conditions on the surface of Venus would allow scientists to float above the fray." Scientists want to actually be able to go to Venus, so they could take actual samples of rock, gas, etc. So, as a result, "many researchers are working on innovations that would allow our machines to last long enough to contribute meaningfully to our knowledge of Venus."

Overall, the author suggests that studying Venus is something that should happen, despite the possibly, dangerous outcome by saying that the challenge of being able to discover Venus isn't "limited by dangers and doubts, but should be expanded to meet the very edges of our imagination and innovation."

An Evaluation of "The Challenge of Exploring Venus"

When writing a persuasive essay authors have a set of guidelines to follow, small things like avoiding first and second person language really help to make an essay good. The author of "The Challenge of Exploring Venus" started off well but quickly made mistakes and went downhill from there. Based on the text the author did not support his idea well because he often used first person language, his paragraphs had no transitions, and for a persuasive writing it was improperly set up.

The first mistake the author made can be found in paragraph one "However, this nickname is misleading since Venus is actually a planet. In our solar system.," the author uses the word "our" which should not be used in a persuasive essay. A better alternative could easily be achieved by replacing "our" for a noun. For example this sentence could be used "In the solar system in which hummanity resides...".

The second mistake cannot be found in paragraphs 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8. Which is where the problem lies, the author makes no attempt at transitioning from paragraph to paragraph. Simple transitions help make an essay easier to read and improve the flow of the essay.

The last mistake the author made was the most drastic. The author did not format his peice as a persuasive essay in any way what so ever. The introductory paragraph starts with an attention grabber and ends with it, the author didn't even try to tie his writing to the audience nor does he include a thesis statement. The body paragraphs that follow don't mention the authors stance and only work to inform readers about trivial facts that only slightly pertain to the arguemnet. Finally the conclusion at least started well, but it suffers from the same problems as the introduction where it is all an attention grabber and nothing else.

Alfonzo Gibraldi once said "You can judge a man for his work or his looks, but you can never judge a man for trying". Gibraldi's quote summarizes the author's work quite well. Although the author did not support his idea well because he used first person language, the paragraphs had no transitions, and it was not properly set up. At least the author tried.

Remember those days when you had to persuade your parents into getting something for you? It may have been a new pair of shoes, a cute little puppy, or maybe even a car. Whatever it was, the goal was to convince them into thinking it was indeed a good idea. You did this by filling their head with as many pros as you can think of, and keeping the cons limited. This same concept applies to supporting an idea in an article. The author's support was not very strong due to the overpowering cons over pros.

The claim that is suggested by the author is "studying venus is a worthy puirsuit despite the dangers it presents". However, we heard very little about why studying venus would be a worthy pursuit. According to the article, "Venus may well once have been the most Earth-like planet in our solar system", so the author could have easily elaborated on how this could be beneficial to humans. Although conditions on Venus today are unfit for human life, it was once probably covered in oceans and supported life.

The last thing you want to do when making a claim is discourage the reader. Yes, the article should touch on the dangers that studying Venus presents but it should not be the main focus of the article. Doing so is just filling the reader's head with more cons than pros on studying Venus and that will not help support your claim at all.

In order to supprt an idea you must bring out the benefits that will encourage your reader to agree. Simply shining the light on the negatives will do the opposite of support your claim. Everything from your title, thesis statement, body, and conclusion should focus on supporting your idea.

In "The Challenge of Exploring Venus," the author strongly explains why the exploration of Venus is a worthy pursuit despite of the dangers and challenges it presents.

Venus is occasionally the closest planet in distance to Earth. Also, its geological composition, density and size, are very similar to Earth. These similarities between Venus and Earth are attracting astronauts and NASA to further explore this planet so more information can be found and analyzed.

As stated by the author, one major challenge of exploring Venus is that its environmental dangers and challenges make it difficult even for spacecrafts to land. "A thick atmosphere of almost 97 percent carbon dioxide", "sulfuric acid in Venus's atmosphere", temperatures "over 800 degrees Farenheit" and atmospheric pressure being "90 times greater" are just some factors that make landing a spacecraft on Venus difficult. Spacecrafts that have been sent to Venus have so far been unmanned since no spacecraft has survived landing for more than a few hours.

Despite several dangers preventing a spacecraft form landing, astronomers are fascinated by Venus's environment as it is believed to have supported forms of life in the past. It even has similar geological features compared to Earth such as valleys, mountains, and craters and was probably covered largely with oceans.These fascinating features call for further exploration which is halted by such difficult challenges and dangers to humans.

In preparation for the future, NASA has created possible solutions which may allow spacecrafts to land on Venus and survive for a couple weeks. The possible solutions being analyzed are designed to avoid unfriendly ground conditions by hovering above the planet. These conditions above the ground are bearable with the right technology, but not survivable for humans. This great challenge is what attracts humans to further explore the planet so they can learn more about its fascinating environment, geological features, and possibly gain more scientific explanation for the unsolved mysteries in science. The author states how obtaining information from Venus may be difficult due to its ground conditions "because most forms of light cannot penetrate the dense atmosphere, rendering standard forms of photography and videography ineffective." Therefore, sending spacecrafts to Venus may have no use since it will be unable to gather pictures and videos. Furthermore, the passage states that, "researchers cannot take samples of rock, gas, or anything else, from a distance." If researchers are not able to land the spacecraft, or the spacecraft cannot survive the dangerous ground conditions, then no samples will be gathered for testing.

The author very clearly explains how humans are struggling to send spacecrafts to Venus and how its dangers and challenges are unbearable. Althought the author shows strong desire to explore Venus and learn more about it, the author does not fully explain the benefits of exploring Venus and how gathering new information from Venus will benefit humankind despite the challenges and dangers faced.

The author does express his fascination and determination to explore Venus when he says, "Our travels on Earth and beyond should not be limited by dangers and doubts but should be expanded to meet the very edges of imagination and innovation." The author sucessfully communicates his hopes of overcoming the dangers and challenges by showing how technology is providing solutions, but there are not as many incentives described. Hence, the author describes the dangers of exploring Venus, but doesn't prove that studying Venus is such a worthy pursuit since the passage has a greater focus on the dangers rather than the outcomes if the challenges are overcome successfully.

Without this knowledge, the reader could not make an educated decision on the issue. After giving the background information, the author introduces the problem. He explains why our "'twin'" planet is so hard to study "despite its proximity to us." (Paragraph 2) Without knowing the information about the dangers of studying Venus, readers would likely not see what the issue was.

The author writes even more information on how inhospitable the planet is. They go into more detail abput the deadly conditions on the planet to make sure the reader understands the extremity of the dangers. They describe "clouds of highly corrosive sulfuric acid," temperatures "averag[ing] over 800 degrees Fahrenheit, and the atmospheric pressure [that] is 90 times greater than what we experience on our own planet." They say why astronomers are "fascinated by Venus" (Paragraph 4) and elaborate on these details. (Paragraph 8) This strong conclusion not only secures his argument but also adds another point in saying that humans will likely attempt other missions that may be even more dangerous, therefore, the experience would gained from studying Venus may be necessary later.

They started by providing information so that the reader could understand the dangers and further built up the counter-argument. The author then presents the issue and his stance to argue for the claim that Venus should be studied regardless of these issues. After doing so, the author provides ways that the dangers could be overcome so that studying the planet would be less challenging. In their conclusion, the author finalizes their argument with another piece of evidence and reaffirms their stance, successfully arguing for the side of exploration of Venus.

The Facial Action Coding System can be an effective teaching tool, and may help teachers in their struggles with getting the message across. By learning the patterns of the face and what works and what doesn't, the computer program can help teach in a more effective manner that is not possible to human instructors. In the article "Making Mona Lisa Smile," by Nick D'Alto, he describes a new type of technology known as the Facial Action Coding System, and how it utilizes a computer software to identify human emotions. Developed by Dr. Thomas Huang, this software was made with the intention of creating better ways for humans and computers to communicate. Dr. Huang also presents the idea of bringing this technology into the classroom, claiming that it can help teachers when a student is confused or growing bored; however, this idea may not be the best way for facilitating the classroom environment. The use of facial scanning technology in a classroom setting in order to read the emotional expressions of the students there will actually bring more negative consequences that outweigh the benefits.

One of the first reasons that must be considered would be this technology could be very expensive. According to D'Alto, the process begins by having the computer construct a 3-D model of the face and, "using video imagery, the new emotion-recognition software tracks these facial movements" in order to identify mixed emotions. This is fairly recent technology, and with the complexity that is required in order for the computer to determine the emotions of the subject, this system could be very expensive for schools to invest in. D'Alto also mentions that, "your home PC can't handle the complex algorithms used to decode Mona Lisa's smile" which thus leads to the conclusion that the complexity of this technology would not suit the computers most schools are able to afford. Thus, the introduction of this technology into the classrooms would not be valuable in the face of finances.

Furthermore, the students' morals must be considered as they may not want their teachers to scan their faces constantly during class. Throughout the article, D'Alto explains how the computers analyze every feature and muscle of the face in order to piece together an analysis, "all 44 major muscles in the model [... are] then associated each with characteristic movements of the facial muscles". Dr. Huang designed the software to be like this because the computers need to be able to recognize the subtle facial movements humans use to express their emotions. By having such an in depth analysis of every small feature on one's face, this may make some of the students uncomfortable, which needs to be put into consideration while deciding whether or not this would benefit the class as a whole. This should also be run by the parents to first see if it is alright with them for a computer to analyze their child's face daily; is it worth this trouble to pick out every emotion a student is conveying? To further expand on this factor, using this technology in order to see how another person is feeling limits the conversation or connection that could have been shared. This could not only reduce the friendliness of the classroom environment, but also how close each student is with each other.

D'Alto goes on, adding that while each emotion remains similar universally, there are still some individuals who "often show varying degrees of expression", therefore, it would vary from student to student, and the accuracy will not be 100% every single run through. While the teachers are able to interact with their students and learn more about how they are feeling through this way, the computer merely scans the students' faces without taking into consideration how their personality, gender, race, age, can affect these results. As D'Alto mentioned, some people tend to smile more easily, while others do not have as broad of a smile. This could lead the facial scanning software to incorrectly analyze the emotions of students, a major downside to incorporating the use of this technology in general.

Finally, by using this facial decoding system, it may also take away from the lessons in class. Not only is it distracting to the students, but it also seems very time consuming to scan every student's facial features. In this situation, human analysis would be the most efficient because it would not have to go through the process of individually calculating what percent of each emotion a student is conveying at the moment. Humans can also detect the quick changes of emotion that students go through during school. Additionally, students could be curious as to how distorting their faces would alter their results of the facial scanning, which would greatly distract them from the learning environment of class. For example, the article states, "In the real smile, the zygomatic major life the corners of your mouth. Meanwhile, muscles called orbicularis oculi pars palpabraeus make crow's-feet around your eyes. But in a false smile, the mouth is stretched sideways using teh zygomatic major and a different msucle, the risorius". This shows that by altering which muscle on the face is contracting, the way the emotions are conveyed would be altered as well. Students could end up playing around with the software by changing these muscular arrangements, and lose the attention that could have been on the teacher's lessons.

Overall, while the Facial Action Coding System is very impressive and is able to read human emotion, replacing simple human analysis of each other would create many more negatives inclucing: the inability to afford this technology in the first place; morals of the students, staff, parents; the accuracy of the software from person to person; as well as the enormous distractions it could cause during class. Thus, the new software that Nick D'Alto has presented in his article, "Making Mona Lisa Smile," presents many attributes that could be useful in certain situations, however in the classroom setting, this would not be the best idea to implement.

Have you ever wondered if someone is truly displaying the emotions they are trying to have you perceive? If so, you'd be interested in learning about the Facial Action Coding System, or FACS. It is a computer algorithm designed to recognize what emotions out of six basic ones-happiness, surprise, anger, disgust, fear, and sadness-using only the muscle movements in a person's face. This technology could be beneficial for use in classrooms to improve both a student's personal and learning experience.

FACS could help instructors determine how engaged students are in a lesson. This is even pointed out in paragraph six of the article "Making Mona Lisa Smile:" "A classroom computer can recognize when a student is becoming confused or bored." This means it can show you who in the class is being engaged and gives instructors an idea if they need to change their lesson plans or not. This will lead to more engaging classes and the more engaging the class is, the more likely it is for students to actually learn.

FACS could help instructors pick out students who seem to be confused with a topic and prompt them to further assist the student. As quoted in the previous paragraph, FACS can pick up on a student's confusion or boredom. Sometimes, students are too afraid to ask for assistance in a class, leading them to begin falling behind in the subject due to their confusion. With FACS, instructors could reach out to assist the students that were displaying confusion to help clarify the subject for them. This can greatly affect a student's grade as well as their understanding for a subject.

The technology in FACS could help school staff determine if a student may need some help dealing with emotional or personal problems. In paragraphs seven and eight, the author implies that FACS can tell the difference between a genuine and a forced smile. It's also stated, in paragraph three, that FACS can also pick up on powerful negative emotions such as anger, fear, and sadness. Being able to pick up on these emotions better could help a student avoid crisis because not everyone can pick up when a person is genuinely happy or faking it. If a student is consistantly forcing their positive emotions, it could prompt a counselor to talk to them and perhaps help the school see if they could help the student in any way. Students may face a lot of troubles in their personal life and the technology that FACS provides could assist school staff to do the best they can to help any student.

From being able to make class more fun to students to helping students with their mental health, FACS provides many benefits in the classroom. With staff being more in sync with students emotions throughout the day, the experience for students in school will improve with the help of the Facial Action Coding System.

Thomas Huang's new system, Facial Action Coding System (FACS), can read human emotions with the latest high technology and has proved to be useful, especially in a classroom setting. Therefore, the class lesson can be modified in order to fit the needs of all students. FACS is incredibly helpful and valuable for schools because it enables everyone to learn with comprehension while adding some fun into the lesson.

With FACS, more students will be able to understand the lesson being taught. In the article, Dr. Huang states, "a classroom computer could recognize when a student is becoming confused." By recognizing if a student is confused, the computer will be able to change the lesson to be more apprehensible. This is extremely valuable to the student because the student will no longer be at a disadvantage; without FACS, a teacher would be oblivious to the fact that a student needed help on a certain concept and thus, the student would not know some information that others would know. This is crucial when the day of a quiz or test comes and that confused student will be unable to answer questions about concepts he had trouble with. Additionally, if some students have a timid personality and cannot speak up in class for help, those students will continue to have the same problem with a concept they do not understand. Dr. Huang says in the article, "A classroom computer could recognize when a student is becoming [...] bored." However, with FACS, the teacher or computer can see that some students are bored, thus leading the teachers or computers to make the lesson more enjoyable. For example, adding in activities that students must partake in or giving out rewards when the students answer the right answer to questions asked about the new lesson will aid students in enjoying the lesson while understanding it at the same time. By reading the emotion of boredom, FACS will allow teachers to evaluate which students are having trouble understanding the lesson, and those students will then be able to fully know the information that was taught due to a lesson alteration that made it more fun.

Since muscles on the face respond to human emotions, even the smallest of movements may evoke a certain feeling that can be caught by the system, something that is very difficult for a human to do. One example of of how a muscle movement may show emotion is, "your frontalis pars lateralis muscle (above your eyes) raises your eyebrows when you're surprsied; your orbicularis oris (around your mouth) tightens your lips to show anger" (3). One's muscle movement tells a lot about what they may be thinking inside, and would take an actor in order to hide this. In everyday circumstances, assuming one does not intend to lie, especially for the purpose of this technology, the Facial Action Coding System can relate the movements accurately to human emotions. According to D'Alto, Dr. Huang created the technology to utilize video imagery in order to track even the smallest of movements (4). Human eyes have their own limits, and may even be limited by one's own lack of attention. Because of this, humans may not be able to catch such small movements, so in this way, this technology can be more powerful than humans in detecting emotions, which proves to be especially useful in a classroom.

One way the Facial Action Coding System can prove valuable to students in a classroom is the ability to input the detection of the emotions into the general system so that it can adjust its actions based of the emotions. Dr. Huang says, "A clasroom computer could recognize [...] then it could modify the lesson, like an effective human instructor" (6). In a circumstance where a teacher may not be available, the computer can act in place of the teacher and may perform with greater accuracy because of its existence as an objective technology with adequate information about the muscles on the face. (muscles that begin at your cheekbones) lift the corners of your mouth" (7). However when someone fake-smiles, "the mouth is stretched sideways using the zygomatic major and a different muscle, the risorius" (8). Learning about this distinction from the way the computer may respond can also help students interact with their friends or classmates. When a classmate feigns happiness, another student can reply in a way that can support the classmate. This technology not only helps students excel academically, but also emotionally, which can ultimately make them better people.

For many students, school is just a building that they are legally required to visit five days a week. However, new technology could change their bleak outlook on their educational system. The Facial Action Coding System (FACS) is a new software that can detect emotions based on facial muscle movements. Using FACS to read the emotional expressions of students in the classroom will be very valuable in the future. This new technology can help students combat depression and stress, better understand their schoolwork, and feel more interested in learning, while preventing students from hiding their true feelings towards their education.

Firstly, moving facial muscles produces emotions, according to the Facial Feedback Theory of Emotion, which is cited in the passage. Having FACS to tell students their emotions will educate them on what facial muscles to move so that they can feel happier and less stressed. FACS will make them more aware of how they are moving their faces, so they can adjust their facial expression to reduce negative feelings. If students feel happier overall, they will be more receptive to educational material, and they may be less likely to suffer from depression. Hence, FACS can lead to more positivity, which can lead to better students.

In addition to helping students feel more joyful when it comes to their education, FACS can also detect when students feel confused so that the lessons can be tailored to individuals to help them understand the material. In the passage, Prof. Thomas Huang stated that in the future, a classroom computer would be able to tell when a student feels confused. Because FACS can show teachers when students do not understand the lessons, teachers can alter their lesson plans or give those specific students extra help to ensure no students are falling behind in their education. Students can then learn more effectively since they will understand the material more.

Moreover, not only can FACS recognize confusion, but it also knows when students are bored. Dr. Huang predicted that classroom computers will eventually be able to recognize students' boredom so that the computers can modify their lessons to keep the students' attention. Students who are bored tend to only complete schoolwork for the sake of completing it, rather than for the sake of their education. If technology can make learning more interesting, students will be more willing to study and learn their material, and, as a result, they will benefit more from their education. Thus, FACS can improve the education system by reducing the boredom students experience and making them more open to learning.

Some skeptics may argue that students could try to hide their emotions by making faces that convey a different emotion than the one they are experiencing, so the technology will not be valuable in determing how students feel. However, the computer software detects even minute facial muscle movements, so students most likely will not be able to fool the software. When someone tries to fake a smile, the zygomatic major and the risorius, which are both facial muscles, stretch the mouth sideways, but in a real smile, the zygomatic major lifts the corners of the mouth and the orbicularis oculi pars palpabraeus makes crow's-feet around the eyes, instead. FACS can detect these small changes in facial expressions, so even the students who are too afraid to ask for help will not be able to hide their confusion or boredom effectively. Teachers can then improved their lessons and help specific students based on information from FACS.

FACS has the potential to make school much more interesting to students by detecting their boredom to help teachers make the necessary adjustments. Additionally, this technology can tell when students are confused, so the lessons can be changed to help them better understand the material. Also, FACS can educate students on their emotional expressions to help them produce feelings of happiness while learning. Finally, FACS can recognize the true emotions of students to inform teachers of ways to alter their teaching methods. With all of its potential benefits considered, FACS will be a valuable addition to the classroom. With new technology in place, education can become more like a hobby and less like an obligation.

Nick D'Alto presents and explains the concept behind new computer technology that can recognize and analyze human emotions in his article "Making Mona Lisa Smile." The article outlines how the software runs and the various benefits of its usage. However, lost in his "selling" of the software, D'Alto fails to recognize that the software is not generally necessary, especially in a classroom setting.

D'Alto makes the claim that the software will be useful to classrooms in that it can help recognize facial expressions, however the use of high-technology computer software to do so is completely unnecessary. D'Alto mentions that this "emotional calculation" is a process that humans experience and use frequently. D'Alto states, "In fact, we humans perform this same impressive 'calculation' every day. For instance, you can probably tell how a friend is feeling simply by the look on her face," (4). He clearly mentions that this computer algorithm recreates the intuitive calculations that humans experience quite often in order to read the emotions of the people around them. Since humans are able to recognize these emotions, the use of a computer to calculate what an instructor is intuitively capable of calculating him or herself is not crucial in any way to the classroom.Huang's argument is that the computer can recognize student emotions and then cater to these emotions by altering the teaching style, "'A classroom computer could recognize when a student is becoming confused or bored... it could modify the lesson, like an effective human instructor.,'" (6) however he fails to keep in mind that this same process is what teachers are already trained to do. Furthemore, the personal connections that instructors foster with their students allows them to take a more insightful approach to reading emotions as they are aware of each individual student's personalized expressions and additional information that can aid them in deciphering student emotions.

Additionally, as with any computerized program or technology overall, the accuracy of this software is not 100 percent, and there is no need to use a possibly inaccurate software in the critical setting of a classroom where students' emotions run high and vary significantly from person to person. The software "improves accuracy in perceiving the emotions of others," (Introduction). While the software may improve accuracy, accuracy cannot be guaranteed. D'Alto's bias towards utilizing this software is clearly shown through continuous praise in the article, however the superiority of the software, presented as only seen through D'Alto's eyes, is questionable considering the software does not even guarantee complete accuracy. Furthermore, as a relatively new software, the computer is only able to recognize six emotions, "Dr. Paul Eckman... has classified six basic emotions-- happiness, surprise, anger, disgust, fear, and sadness," (3). There are an infinite number of emotions considering mixed emotions and emotions that cannot be conveyed through facial expressions, and reducing this myriad of complex emotions down to six would be a disservice. If the software is only able to recognize these six basic emotions, a person's emotional range is reduced down to six possible emotions and the software would not be able to comprehend more complex emotions that fall outside these six basic emotions. D'Alto states that the software works through comparison to an emotionless face, "Each expression is compared against a neutral face (showing no emotion)," (4). The software uses a neutral face to determine emotions based on facial expression, but individuals have a variety of neutral faces. Some people have neutral expressions that appear to convey emotions but it's actually just their natural emotionless visage. In order to truly evaluate against a neutral face, the software would need to store data based on the neutral face of every subject that it later analyzes in order to compare them to their true neutral face rather than a predetermined one. Due to its lack of complete accuracy, small range of recognizable emotions, and use of a so-called "neutral face" that may not be neutral to some individuals at all, the FACs is not completely accurate and therefore serves no purpose in the classroom.

However, this does not go to say that FACs is entirely useless, as it can still provide its service to other areas, besides the classroom, where it will actually be useful. D'Alto states that Huang observes that artists use the same methods of deducing emotions through carefully analyzing human anatomy of the 44 facial muscles. The article states, "artists such as da Vinci studied human anatomy to help them paint facialmuscles precisely enough to convey specific emotions," (5). As the computer software uses these same skills, artists who are not as experience could utilize the software to analyze the emotions of subjects in other paintings and begin honing their facial analytical skills. The software can also aid designers in better animation, "the same technology can make computer-animated faces more expressive-- for video games or video surgery," (6). This technology can really help design reach new levels through its facial data and analytics. Nevertheless, the software serves no purpose in a classroom setting. While there are useful applications for the technology in art and design fields, it does not need to be implemented in the classroom.

All in all, the computer software, while bringing technology to new heights and pushing the bounds on technological capabilities, the extent of its usefulness does not reach schools and their classrooms. Classrooms do not need expensive computer software to replicate student analysis that can be easily done, and on a more personal level, by an instructor. The software has its drawbacks, and placing a potentially inaccurate software in the classroom does not seem to be the best idea. Needless to say, this computer software is unnecessary in the classroom, however can be very useful in its application to artists and designers and allocating resources to people who can get the most out of this software is wiser than placing it in a classroom where it will either go unused or inaccurately read students. According to the Facial Action Coding System, a new software that is said to accurately percieve human emotions, the Mona Lisa is "83 percent happy, 9 percent distinguished, 6 percent fearful, and 2 percent angry." This mysterious facial expression that humans have been trying to decode for centuries has been easily broken down by this software; but how accurate is this analysis? And how would this kind of software be useful? According to Nick D'Alto, we can use this to benefit academics by programming it into school computers that would read students' emotions and react by shifting a lesson plan to personal preference. However, the Facial Acting Coding System, while an impressive feat of analytical technology, would not be valuable to students in a classroom setting because the computer could misread emotions, could be a disadvantage in the classroom by eliminating collaboration, and expecially young children could become distracted by the software.

In a classroom filled with people who are teenagers or younger, this technology would find itself making many mistakes. This is not because the software program itself has issues, but rather these mistakes would occur due to the emotions that young people experience. If a child is sad, they probably would not react positively to learning anything academically related, so the computer wouldn't detect any emotions of happiness from the child based on their facial expression. In another scenario, a child might already dislike what they are learning; they would once again react negatively to the lesson as a whole because they don't find the content useful or engaging. In both situations, the computer would have no feedback from the students to shift the lesson plan, rendering it useless. This problem would occur especially in very young children who constantly react emotionally to a surplus of triggers and situations throughout the day that could affect how accurately the computer reads their emotions. Similarly, even in older children and adults, other life situations could impact a person's attitude towards their education momentarily, once again rendering the system useless.

Another disadvantage of using a system like this in a classroom setting is its inevitable elimination of collaboration. Working with others is an important skill that is especially emphasized by the process of going to school. Online school is a much more easily accessible alternative to physically going to school, but socialization in a classroom environment is the reason why many people continue to go to school. After their education is over, most jobs are very collaborative and involve talking and working with others as a means of accomplishing something more important than a science project or english essay. It would be impossible for a single person to effectively run an entire hospital; collaboration is essential. A system like the Facial Acting Coding System would eliminate this important interaction because the lessons would become increasingly tailored to individual interests. If everyone in the classroom is learning based on their personal preferences, how are they all supposed to come together and collaborate? While it is important to acknowledge that people learn in different ways, it is more important to make sure that collaboration is still enforced above all, and this system would not effectively do so.

Children are not fully matured and often do not quite understand the purpose of education. The rapid increase in technology has created seemingly limitless possibilities for the future; however, this rise is accompanied humans pressing toward the boundaries of numerous ethicial and moral standards. One such ethical line that could be crossed in the near future is the privacy of an individual. We are reaching a society where in time, it would be feasible to monitor every single living human on earth at the exact same time. With this in mind, people are asking themselves the question of where would the boundary be between the invasion of an individual's privacy and the collective good a worldwide security system could be. In his article, "Making Mona Lisa Smile," Nick D'Alto outlines new software that could, if further enhanced, allow students' facial expressions to be read during classrooms. Then it could modify the lesson, like an effective human instructor" (6). When digging deeper, however, there are a lot of risks and ethical boundaries that are being crossed if this technology were further developed.

In order for the Facial Action Coding System to be able to determine a person's emotion, according to paragraph 3, it must first scan a person's face and render a 3D model of the face wtih all the facial muscles in the face. Then the machine can use this model to determine through muscle movement the emotional expression of the person. This sounds amazing; however, there are many security implication with this technology, specifically the need to scan a person's face. This software needs to construct a very realistic 3-D model of the face, and it has to use this 3-D to determine a person's muscle position. Therefore, this software would need to save this person's facial expression and then analyze, but there are some security risks with having a machine save and analyze students' facial expressions. If a security breach were to happen in the school, every single human in the school would now have their face accessible by the infiltrator. This is a very serious risk to many people who wish to not have arguably the most personal information stolen from them. The face is seemingly the last defense against identity theft and crimes of those sorts. With facial recognition software being stolen, many people would be facing serious risk of being hacked or other crimes. Even if the computer did not store the face, an infiltrator could bug the computer and have every person's face when being analyzed also feed into their private computer. The possibilities for security breaches are just too much of a risk to allow this technology inside a classroom.

Some supporters of this technology might argue that humans also analyze emotions and it is not different if a machine does it as the machine just does it better. Unfortunately, this is not the case. Like what Dr. Huang said, "humans perform this same 'impressive' calculation every day. For instance, you can probably tell how a friend is feeling simply by the look on their face " (5). But Dr. Huang does not realize that humans do not create a 3-D model of each person's face. Humans do not keep copies of every person's face that they have met. As humans, people forget stuff easily, but that is not the same with computer who can accurately keep an exact copy of everything they see.

If the Facial Action Coding System were implimented inside a classroom, it would also be in constant obserbance of everyone. This would be a major ethical breach as it would almost universally be considerd invasion of privacy. Unlike other old technology such as security cameras, this machine would have to be constantly analyzing every person's emotion in order to determine whether students understand or not. This is because as Dr. Huang said, "A classroom computer could recongize when a student is becoming confused or bored... Then it could modify the lesson, like an effective human instructor" (6). However, for this to be able to work well, the computer would need inputs from the students all the time. For many, imagining their faces being analyzed constantly during school would not be fun. It would put immense pressure on the students to pay attention and do well in the class as they are constantly being observed. This pressure and all-knowing eye (the computer) would in the long term, be detrimental to the students' performance as many will be burned out by the immense scrutiny the machine places on them to look like their paying attention and to look not confused. They can only objectify and analyze through numbers. Unlike what Dr. Huang said, "So computers need to understand [nonverbal comuncation, too" (6), computers can not understand faces. They only can crunch numbers and give percentages.

In conclusion, the Facial Action Coding System should not be implemented inside a classroom. This is because it is a risk to people's security due to its storing of people's faces and how it can observe everyone at the same time in an act of privacy invasion. While the invention is a marvelous thing, they are numerous changes that need to be made in order for it to be classroom friendly and safe. Machines are the future of the new world. In today's world, technology like this is already being put into place, but on the smaller scale of simple facial recognition. At home, people could use this software to better their internet use by providing more information to let companies know which ads you like, for example, "if you smile when a Web ad appears on your screen, a similar ad might follow. The Facial Action Coding System (or FACS) is a software application that allows the computer to be able to read the facial expressions of humans. This application could prove to be very valuable if used in classrooms. According to paragraph 6 of the article, "A classroom computer could recognize when a student is becoming confused or bored...Then it could modify the lesson, like an effective human instructor." This ability could be very useful in classes, as it would create a more individualized lesson for each student's pace, as well as keep the student involved and interested in what they are learning.

Teachers generally have classes of about 25-30 kids, all learning the same thing at the same time in the same room. Because teachers have a limited amount of time to teach their lesson, it's difficult for them to be able to determine whether or not every individual is understanding the subject. They simply don't have time to walk the students through it individually. However, with the use of FACS on student computers, individualized curriculum may be possible.

By reading the student's facial expressions, the computer would be able to determine if the student was actually understanding the lesson. If they were not, the computer might offer more step-by-step examples for them, to see if that helps them understand. By doing this, the computer is able to help the student learn properly. However, what makes it so convenient is that the rest of the class didn't have to see the extra examples. The kids who already understand the curriculum don't have to wait on the kids who are struggling. This way everyone learns at the pace that is right for them, and nobody has to worry about trying to keep up as the rest of the class moves on while they're still trying to understand the fundamentals.

Computers would also be able to keep students interested in the lesson. Teachers try their best to keep everyone involved, but sometimes kids will ignore them anyways, because they find the particular topic or lesson boring. The computer would be able to use FACS to recognize that the student is not paying attention or doesn't care, and would be able to change the way the lesson was being taught to that individual in order to make the topic more interesting. Again, the rest of the class is not affected by these changes, so nobody else is bothered.

Some people might argue that teachers can read expressions just as well as a computer might. While that may be true in some cases, most people tend to base others' expressions on their instinct and past experiences. In paragraph 5, it's stated that "Of course, most of us would have trouble actually describing each facial trait that conveys happy, worried, etc." This is because most people don't take the time to determine what exactly makes up a happy face and what makes up a sad one. We often use the context of the situation, as well as assumptions and instinct, to judge someone's mood and expression.

Computers are able to judge someone's expression based on a set algorithm. They hold no biases or assumptions, only exact calculations that determine somebody's mood based on their face. For example, people sometimes say things like "he has an angry face," when describing someone (even though the person in question is not actually mad) because his emotionless face still looks "angry" to them. Computers would be less likely to make these assumptions, because the program knows exactly what muscles make up an "angry face", and does not use instinct to judge someone's expression.

In short, the use of technology to determine the facial expressions of students in the classroom would be very valuable. FACS judges facial expressions based on the muscles that move in the face (it does not operate based on impressions and assumptions like humans do). The computers would be able to individualize lesson plans for students who are struggling (or, conversely, students who are flying through the class). Computers could also make lessons more interesting for students who are not paying attention, so they can become more involved in the lesson without holding up the whole class to do so. Through the implementation of FACS on school computers, students could be able to make the most out of their educational experience in the classroom.

Miscommunication is often the root of many problems. It occurs when people do not reveal their true intentions or emotions about a subject. This is prominent in both home life and school life, and can be difficult to overcome. To combat miscommunication, professors from the University of Illinois and the University of Amsterdam have created a new software, the Facial Action Coding System, which determines the emotions of others. This technology is very valuable and should be used in classrooms because it will benefit a student's academics, create relationships between students, and improve teacher and student interactions.

To begin with, the Facial Action Coding System will benefit a student's academics greatly. It is common that students become distracted during online lessons. Dr. Huang explains how this system can improve the student's activity. He says that it "could recognize when a student is becoming confused or bored...then it could modify the lesson". This component would be extremely beneficial to each student, because the computer would be able to individualize each student's lessons. Thus, each student could learn items at his or her own pace, without the stress of a generalized plan that does not measure the feelings of each student. This way, each student could have a personal "human instructor" who could teach the student. Furthermore, this system can help in student productivity, since the system can place items in your computer that will make a person smile. The Facial Feedback Theory of Emotion believes that "moving your facial muscles...may even help produce them", so these tailored advertisements can lead to actually cheering a student up. Thus, this will improve academic performance because the student will perfom better when they are in a pleasant mood.

To continue, this system will help to create and better invaluable relations between students, resulting in a friendlier and more productive classroom environment. During conversations in the classrooms, some kids are very vocal and voice their opinions, but there are students who are shy and choose not to speak. This technology can aid those students by decoding their expressions. The author writes about how the computer can do this: "classified six basic emotions...associated each with characteristic movements of the facial muscles". The computer can determine the students thoughts on a topic, and then translate it to his or her peers, who can interact through the information delivered. Also, fights between students are fairly common. A student involved in a conflict may not reveal his or her feeling due to stubborness or fear. The author explains how most people "would have trouble actually describing each facial trait". However, the system can do that, and will be able to detect the student's thoughts. By doing this, there can be a faster route to solving the problem. Therefore, by utlitizing this system, it can promote healthier relationships between students, resulting in a calmer classroom setting. As a result, it will improve a student's attention and focus.

Furthermore, this new techology can improve relationships between students and teachers. A teacher's primary role is to teach the student, and a student's primary role is to learn the material or raise awareness if he or she cannot comprehend it. Unfortunately, there are instances in which a student feels ashamed and does not ask for help. Teachers can use this software to determine if a student is feeling frustrated towards a specific topic. For example, the computer can determine if the subject is using "your orbicularis oris (around your mouth) [which] tightens your lips to show anger". This can be transcribed to the teacher, who then works with the student to solve the issue. Therefore, it will increase academic performance as well as strengthen emotional stability. In addition, this system can help improve a student's mental wellbeing if the teacher is able to detect it with help of the system. A student may be struggling with issues outside of the classroom. A teacher can help confirm this with the software, and work with the student to determine the problem. An additional benefit is that "the software can even identity mixed emotions". This will help solidify the issues a student is experiencing, since the software will tell various emotions instead of a single emotion. Thus, this technology will be important because it will improve student-teacher relationships by raising both academic and emotional concerns.

In conclusion, the Facial Action Coding System is invaluable to a classroom and should be utilized on a daily basis. It will aid and personalize each student's academic track, allowing him or her to learn in the best possible way. It will improve interactions in between students, resulting in better teamwork. Finally, it will strengthen relations between students and teachers. All in all, this new technology must be applied to classrooms because it will decrease miscommunication between people. As a result, a healthier and more productive classroom environment will emerge.

Technology has always been evolving. From the first consumer computers in the 1980's, to the mainframe era of the past decades, to the complicated and complex computers we have today, technology has always been getting more advanced. Yet, at each rung in the ladder of technology, there has always been new technologies claiming to be the "next greatest thing," but falling short of just that.

In this latest step of technology evolution, people have began to develop AI--artificial intelligence--in order to learn like humans, be like humans, and recognize patterns like humans. The Facial Action Coding System is one of these latest AIs, developed by Professor Thomass Huang of the Beckman Institute for Advanced Science in the University of Illinois, and claiming to be the next greatest thing in the classroom, being able to read student's emotional expressions in the learning environment and react accordingly. Yet, Huang's technology is a double-edged sword. The use of facial emotion recognization in the classroom is a misguided attempt at innovation in technology, and will only lead to an invasion of privacy and increased expenses due to processing power requirements; additionally, people who argue that this technology will help students learn clearly do not recognize the problems in conflict with traditional classrooms and effectiveness.

The use of facial emotion recognization in the classroom will not be a valuable tool, and instead will lead to an invasion of privacy and a conflict with laws. Facial recognition would require sensors everywhere, namely cameras constantly focused on the student. As Huang says himself, emotional "communication is nonverbal [...] so computers need to understand that" (Paragraph 6). In order to improve software products, user input is almost always required. Much of the software used today follows this type of mindset. When programs crash, they send data of the user and what they are doing to the product creator. Thus, a facial recognization program, in order to improve its accuracy and "understand [emotions]", would need to send data about the user to the programmer. At its best, this would be simple information about what is on the computer. At its worst, this would lead to a big-brother like state in schools, with pictures being sent constantly. However, most likely, the product will send pictures whenever the programmer wants to improve their product. Whichever of these situations occurs, a violation of privacy is automatically in place, even if it is just sending small amounts of information about the computer, as not all students would consent. Laws already exist to prevent all of these collections of data on children, laws such as COPA, which would prove a massive problem to facial recognization in attempts to improve software, enough of a problem to completly kill off facial recognization in the classroom.

The use of facial emotion recognization in the classroom is not a valuable tool, and will fail due to the lack of technologic powers and increased cost. Although emotion recognization seems to be a great, bleeding-edge tool which will help with the future, one of its fundamental flaws is the technology required. As mentioned by the author, "your home PC can't handle the complex algorithms used" in the facial recognization process (Paragraph 7). Therefore, how can schools, many without proper funding for technology, be expected to meet the technologic requirements for running facial recognization? They can't. Even with the previous trend of exponential growth in the complexity of technology, schools will not be able to meet the needs to facial recognization. Modern-day computers that run the technology are very advanced, costing thousands of dollars. With the rising prices of technology and the decreasing rate of growth in the complexity of technology, facial recogization will become something that only expensive computers can run. The truth is, many schools run on very outdated technology and cannot afford to buy new expensive computers simply for one task. One might suggest that governments completly cover the cost of technology for public and private schools, but this would provide a massive burden on the US, having to provide hundreds of thousands of computers, and expensive ones too. This cost would be better spend on providing education for people in need, rather than more novelties and niceties for priviledged students. Additionally, only a few large companies supply learning products to schools. With this type of facial recognization, there would be little competition due to the complex nature required to code and run the product. With less competition, monopolization of a product becomes easier, which would drive costs up more.

Although some people may argue that the use of facial emotion recognization in the learning environment is valuable and could help boost student's learning, they clearly do not see the potential for abuse and conflict with classroom types; nor do they see the key problem with facial recognization in the classroom: the simple fact that it has not been proven effective. Modern day classrooms are simple: the teacher teaches, the student sits and learns. This method has not changed for decades, despite the advancement of technology. New tech may provide some form of online learning, but most students still partipate in a traditional classroom. Due to this, the use of tech may help students learn, but tech is typically not the only things students learn from. Teachers still exist to help. However, with facial recognization, schools would require students to be constantly on technology, with software constantly gauging their learning rates, "recogniz[ing] when a student is becoming confused or bored" (Paragraph 6). This would invalidate the traditional classroom setting, making teachers obsolete. A shift in how classrooms are operated would be required, a shift that many people are reluctant to do. Additionally, some students would not benefit as well from learning on computers. Some students learn verbally. Some graphically. Some with their hands. Some students simply cannot learn with technology, or have hard time doing so. Using facial recognization would provide a disvantage to these students. However, all of this ignores the one most major problem of facial recognization in the learning environment: the fact that it has not been scientifically proven. Studies have been run on how facial cues impact emotion, such as the "Facial Feedback Theory of Emotion" which suggest that "moving your facial muscles not only expresses emotions, but also may help produce them" (Paragraph 9). Yet, no studies have been run on how facial recognizing would benefit, or not benefit, students in the classroom.

Facial emotion recognization in the classroom is not a valuable technology for use for students in the classroom due to privacy invasions, cost, and not being scientifically studied. In order to improve the software, privacy would have to be invaded in order to improve accuracy rates and prevent software errors. The cost of such technology would be massive, requiring computers that have massive amounts of processing power, a cost that schools and governments cannot afford. This cost can be put to other things than facial recognization in the classroom. Likewise, facial recognization has not even been scientifically tested to work in the classroom. People who suggest that facial recognization could help in the classroom do not realize these fallacies preventing it from working. Even though technology has been evolving, facial recognization in the classroom is simply another technology that will not work and will die out, as have many other technologies that people have claimed to be the next greatest thing.

Teachers are responsible for test scores and making sure their students are working hard in the classroom, however, the student holds a majority of the power over their success. Education is extreamly important and most would agree that it is the key to a successful life. However, using technology to constantly monitor student's emotions toward the lessons is to extreme. Additionally, if the teacher was teaching the lesson, it would be clear to the instructor if class was engaged in the lesson or not, without the use of computer data to validate the student's emotions. Overall, despite the intrest the student has in the topic of the lesson being learned, if the student really cared about their success in the course, they would learn the material despite the lack of entertainment provided in doing so.

People have bad days, and sometimes they simply cannot focus on a lesson. This does not mean they need to be penalized for becoming distracted or bored. The student is responsible for learning the material or asking for assistance. Every student becomes bored or confused during lessons at some point in their educational pathway. It is the student's responsibility to ask the instructor for assistance or further clarification if they do not understand the content being taught. A computer should not automatically be able to detect the confusion or lack thereof of a student in order to alter the lesson or alert an instructor. It should be the job of the student to determine when they become confused enough to ask for assistance. This is caused by your frontalis pars lateralis muscle (which is above your eyes). On the other hand, if you're feeling a bit angered or agitated, your orbicularis oris (or around your mouth in other words) can begin to tighten your lips to show it.

You reassure her that everyone is a bit forgetful at times, and you help her gather her belongings as she walks back out the door, this time heading to the correct destination. A boy gladly rises from his spot and slides into the seat next to him, laughing and smiling as he strikes up a conversation with his newfound buddy. Now, as you head back to your desk to start the day out, you notice that everyone else is laid back as could be, with not a care in the world with how they're feeling. You can now start the day out right with a clear head, knowing you made a great difference today.

Imagine taking an online lesson, slowly becoming more and more bored, then suddenly without any warning, your entire lesson dynamic switches to become more fun. Such was the intent of Professor Thomas Huang from the Beckman Institute for Advanced Science at the University of Illinois. Prof. Huang created a computer program that can detect emotion in a human through a facial recognition simulator. Essentially, this program can "read" someone's emotion based on the small hints our faces give away when we react to something. However, this system could be problematic.

Firstly, using computers to detect emotions could be problematic in the sense that computers can't necessarily understand human emotion. Although small triggers in our faces could give emotion away, these don't always inherently dictate our mood. For instance, in doing any assignment, one may come across as bored in their facial expression, which is normal. This doesn't necessarly mean that a student needs a new way of learning, it could be a combination of environmental factors that have nothing to do with an assignment itself. Therefore, switching the lesson plan may only confuse a student further or cause anger. Should a computer read an emotion wrong, the student would be the one that suffers, which is why technology is not always trustworthy on something that is human instinct.

Furthermore, the value of a student's emotion in a classroom, although important, doesn't automatically mean the student should be tended to immediately. We, as humans, need to learn how to balance our emotions and handle them effectively in a workplace, which school prepares us for. However, if our school computer reads our emotions constantly, it could cause us to have a warped sense of the real world. As adults, we will not be "babied" everytime our feelings are hurt, and therefore we shouldn't be taught that we will be. Admittedly, there is a line where intervention may be appropriate in regards to one's emotion, however that's what we rely on friends and family for. If we trust our computer as our confidant, we may grow to lack human connection later in life.

One may argue that computers detecting emotion may be a good thing. This could detect early signs of depression or anxiety, and therefore we could take precautions against such things. A computer could be handy when a student is too scared to speak up about being bullied or speak up about something happening at home. Again, though, we can't rely on computers to do everything for us. Our communication skills are dying out at an alarming rate due to new technology; in result we don't use them as we should. Children and especially teenagers are quickly learning that devices can do anything for them; therefore adding another innate human quality to that could be harmful to one's sense of humanity.

In conclusion, although helpful in many fields and practices, this system is not valuable in school. This system admittedly has it's perks, however the flaws definitely outweigh them. It is necessary that we keep means of communication alive, and we give children real, human resources to discuss their feelings. If humans rely on electronics to deal with emotions, we may just turn into electronics ourselves.
