Imagine that while you take an online lesson a computer could change what is being displayed to you depending on the emotion you are showing.

This is exactly what could be possible with the Facial Action Coding System (FACS).

FACS reads the facial expression you are displaying and can act upon it.

However the use of FACS to read the emotional experssions of students is not valuable or beneficial because of many reasons, these include making a lesson that will change depending on what emotion is displayed is not practical, outward expressions are not always what people are feeling, and very few students will have access to this computers that can run this type of software.

It is very hard and tedious to make online-only lessons that are challenging and teach something while also being accessible to everyone that is learning it.

If a online school system decided to employ this software into all of their lessons, the programmers and teachers need to essentially set up tens, if not hundreds, of different lessons for what would normally be one simple lesson.

If the online school is set up as a slideshow, or uses different pages the student can click through to learn, and there is originally ten slides, each slide now needs to have atleast ten different versions (1A-10A) for the first slide of information.

Then, if a student is on the slide 3A, there needs to be atleast ten different versions of slide B correspond with slide A, (example would be 3A would then go to something like 8B3A) that is now a hundred and ten different slides made.

By the time the student would reach the last slide (slide J) there would need to be ten billion different slides made for just the last slide a person would see (Slide J).

That is extremely impractical and might as well be impossible. Not to mention if the online lesson was a video and needed to change itself as the video played.

Outward expressions are not always reflective of inner emotions and thoughts. For example, a teenager could always have a straight face on for most scenarios.

This student could be really enjoying the lesson but they just have a straight face.

The computer would detect this student to be bored and keep trying to entertain the student and progressively be more 'fun'.

This could be extremely annoying to the student who was greatly enjoying and learning well from the lesson but since they did not show happiness on their face the computer kept changing how the lesson was taught.

The student would then, for every single other lesson they take using the facial software, have to constantly keep a happy 'content' face on even if it is more work and distracts them from the lesson.

Even if a lesson can have billions of different slides and even if the software can outsmart a persons 'normal' face and detect that as being content, there is no way a student could be able to even have this technology.

The first sentence in paragraph seven states "Your home PC can't handle the complex algorithms used to decode Mona Lisa's smile".

In 2018 most people that have a home PC build it from the ground up to be as powerful as it can be on the market, if a home PC in 2006 cannot decode the smile of a still image, it is highly doubtful a 2018 home PC could decode a real face at real time and self update lessons.

Even if a PC for the house could be built able to run that line of code it will be far too expensive for any student to afford.

If a student could afford a PC and afford however much the school would charge to use such a huge and resource demanding program (remember they had to design ten billion slides so the tuition to the school just got much more expensive) they still are required to be streaming their face to the school at all times, which is a huge security risk, and need to constantly have an internet connection that is better than what is available in most places to stream the face code.

There are some people who would point out that such a feature could be optional only to enhance an experience not rely on it, or that a public free school could pay for devices to run that.

The latter point falls apart very quickly as there is no need for a face scanning program at a public high school where there is an actual teacher.

Nor is there anyway a government funded school could afford a handful of PCs that could run that software, much the less laptops (there is no laptop currently in the world that could anyway) schools traditionally hand out to students.

The first point has more grounding, the idea of having that as just an option to those who have the internet and PC hardware to use it sounds very attractive.

However, this becomes much less attractive when price is brought up again.

The students that could run such a program are in the minority that the only way money would not be lost is if the students that use it pay extra, which would be like ten thousand dollars atleast, or if every student has to pay a couple extra thousand.

Neither of these options would go over well and a very large sum of money would end up lost.

In conclusion, the idea of a face reading software sounds great on paper but falls apart very quickly when having to put it in practice.

Each individual lesson would need to have billions of slides made for it to accomodate for changing emotions.

Outward expressions do not always reflect inside emotions a person is feeling and the computer has no way to know that.

As well as there being very few students could afford the hardware, internet, tuition to have this software available.

With all these reasons stated the Facial Action Coding System might have many practical uses and places to be, but a classroom is not one of those.

Dr. Huang believes that this system could be used in schools to help advance the use of technology in the classroom. When a student is confused the computer could change the lesson, on only that students computer, in order for that student to be able to understand the content presented. The FACS machine could alleviate all the question asking and sleeping in classrooms by keeping the students engaged in what they're learning about.

For example, if you smile when a Web ad appears on your screen, a similar ad might follow. But if you frown, the next ad will be different." D'Alto uses the example of advertisements as a way to detect emotions through the computer -- in this case if the person liked the ad, then more ads similar to the previous ad would appear; but if the person did not like the ad, then the next ad would be different. This could also be used in the classroom. The computer could analyze the emotions of the student and could keep the student on task. For example, if a student were playing games during a lesson, the FACS machine would be able to detect that through the student's emotions and would put the student back to the lesson. This would allow the teacher to be sure that all students are paying attention and on task during the lesson.

The computer can tell whether a person is actually smiling or giving a forced smile by looking into the muscular action units. For example, a teacher asks her student if he is enjoying the lesson. The student responds by lying, "Yes, it's very fun," but in reality the student does not enjoy the task. Through the FACS, the teacher would be able to spot that the kid is bored and that he was showing fake emotion to her. I do not believe that the use of this technology is in anyway practical to read students' emotional expressions.

I think this for a couple of reasons. The first one is that, when does this ever see use? In the article it talks about a computer teaching a class, analyzing the emotions of the students, and modifying the lesson to accomadate them. But the issue is, computers do not soley teach classes. It's 2018, we still use teachers to teach. Maybe if this technology was implemented in classes, we would replace teachers with computers, but this starts a whole other list of issues.

For a minute, lets say that computers do teach classes, and lets avoid the issues that this alone brings for now. Let's say that the computer decides to scan everyone's face. What happens if someone is not in the classroom, or if they simply aren't looking at the computer? This causes the statistics of the classes emotions to be skewed, and then the class is not acurately accomadated for.

The article states, "Your home PC can't handle the complex algorithms used to decode Mona Lisa's smile." Does this mean normal PC's cannot handle this progream altogether? If so, how expensive are these super PC's? Schools may not be able to afford a PC that can handle this program.

Back to the skewing of results. I can almost certainly say that their will be students who hide their emotions. They may not even do it on purpose. For instance, if someone has a straight face, but is still happy, then the computer will misread the emotion and mess up the results. The number one issue with this program being used in a class is that they go off of hard muscle data, they cannot "read" the room. A human being teacher can almost certainly "read" the room, and understand another human's emotions much better than a computer can. Human teachers have more data to go off of than simply muscle contractions. They can see the context of situations, and know if someone is happy even though they aren't specifically smiling. Going purely off of one source of data is foolish, and would not result in anything good.

There is another issue, similar to hiding emotions. It is extremely easy to fake emotion as well. People do it everyday, and if a computer could not differentiate the difference between genuine and fake emotion, this would be exploitable by the class. I'm assuming that, because it goes strictly off of muscle contractions, it could not tell the difference between real and fake emotions, and this would cause many mistakes. Let's say that a class is really not enjoying their lesson, but it is very easy and do not want it to change. In order to do this, all they have to do is pretend to be happy, even though really they are bored. The computer could not tell this, and would continue with the easy, but boring lesson.

The issues don't only arise from the program itself, though. If a teacher is not present, and only a computer is teaching, how does the computer keep order? Now you could say that a human is present as well, but I am going off of the text in the passage, "Then it could modify the lesson, like an effective human instructor." This sentence insinuates that the computer would be replacing the human, as it is an effective replacement. If a teacher is not present, their will be no order in the classroom. How does a computer stop someone from just leaving the class? Or bullying another student? Current AI is no where near the level needed to fully replace a human teacher.

In conclusion, although the program may sound fun and interesting, current day technologies simply do not allow it to be practical in a classroom. It presents many more problems than solutions, and this makes it impractical. It would be more useful as a "gag" for a single day, just to provide some entertainment with how poorly it performs. Until AI is advanced enough to fully replicate and replace a human being, this technology will never be useful in a classroom.

This is because of a new technology, the Facial Action Coding System, that "tracks these facial movements" (D'Alto 4). It uses a computer algorithm to monitor the emotions of people, then it can reveal how exactly the person is feeling based off "movement of one or more muscles" (D'Alto 3). It may seem far fetched, but use of this technology has the possibility of improving the classroom experience for millions of children around the world.

The use of this FACS technology in the classroom revolves around adapting lesson plans as they are being taught. Thomas Huang, a professor at the University of Illinois, said, "A classroom computer could recognize when a student is becoming confused or bored. Then it could modify the lesson, like an effective human instructor." (D'Alto 6). His logic makes sense, and implementing this technology could have a profound impact on students around the world. Think of all the children who struggle because of the pace or difficulty of a class. Those children may not have the financial resources for a tutor or the willingness to ask the teacher. But by using this technology to address confusion, the students' understanding of the content will strengthen. However, the benefits don't stop at the children.

Teachers all around the world can improving their educating methods by interpreting the data of their students. A teacher who is using this technology may see that 75% of her/his students made confused faces when confronted with problem #7 on the homework. The teacher may choose to review that subject the next day with all of her/his students.

Also, the use of this technology could lead to a more enjoyable classroom experience. There are many positives with being aware of a student's confusion. But several advantages may also arise from being aware of their boredom. If most students in a classroom understand a subject, but are bored with it, the teacher may see this data and choose to move on to new material. This avoids wasting time on content that the students are proficient in, and increases the morale of the students. Learning a new exciting topic may give energy to these students.

Looking back at all of the benefits of utilizing this technology, it would be reasonable to say that FACS has the potential to benefit schools around the globe if used correctly. Implementing FACS in schools can lead to higher student morale, more proficient student comprehension, and an overall more enjoyable school experience. Students can be guided back on to the right track when they begin to get confused. Students can also be pushed a little bit harder when things begin to become too easy. Eliminating confusion and promoting enjoyable learning can have profoud effects on schools. These would become schools filled with students that love to learn. If FACS were to see these smiling faces, it would deduce that the subjects are "100 percent happy."

Such advancemnt can even detect one's mood, such as Prof. Thomas Huang's algorithm that can identify a person's mood based solely on a photograph. While such technology exists, it does raise the question of whether or not it should be used to read the emotions of students. This emotional expression reading technology should not be used to identify the emotions of students due to the obvious invasion of privacy and the effect it could potentially have on teachers across the country.

Having the ability to read a student's emotions is an obvious invasion of privacy. While students forfeit some of their rights at the doors of their schools, despite having fought for them in famous cases like TLO v. The State of New Jersey, the ability to read their emotions takes this lack of privacy that we have to a whole new level. Not only this, but the software even has the capability of "identify[ing] mixed emotions". This means that it can detect more than just one emotion at a time. Unlike other invasions of privacy, such as a school's ability to drug test freely, or the student body's capability to be subject to random searches to protect the school from drugs, weapons, and other paraphanelia, the ability to scan the students' emotions has no real arguement to support it in the interest of forfeiting even more of students' privacy rights.

While the invasion of the students' privacy is one reason against implementing this technology into schools, another reason is the disastorous effect that it could have on the teachers. A teacher's salary and bonus is already dependent enough on students, whether it be how they perfrom on the next standardized test or how their grades improve or what they score on pre-tests at the begining of the year. If this technology were to be implemented into schools, then it would have the potential to devolve into yet another thing our teacher's ability to make ends meet depends on. With the ability to detect a student's displeasure during a certain class, the teacher's pay would be greatly effected. This, along with waging salary with students' grades, is unfair to the teachers, as some students will simply not perform as well as others on standardized tests, just like some students simply do not get along with their teachers, and to penalize for this would be unjust.

While having this technology to scan old paintings and even your friends may be fun, to mandate its use in classrooms would be unjust. Having the capability to create and expand the limits of technology does not necessarily mean that one should. This technology, although inivative, should not be used on students.

For the past decade, we've been relying on computers and technology more than ever in personal life, the workplace, and, especially, classrooms across the world. We use projectors to display images, work problems out on the board and show video. We use laptops for quizzes, tests, and essays. We even use technology to sharpen our pencils and power the rooms we learn in. Because of this, it is almost indisputable that introducing groundbreaking new technology into the classroom leads to a better learning experience; schools invest large amounts of money into these technologies, and this is the reason developing technologies such as the Facial Action Coding System are so important.

The Facial Action Coding System, or FACS, is a technology developed by Professor Thomas Huang of the Beckman Institute for Advanced Technology at the University of Illinois, with the promise of applications in many industries, but primarily education. The technology allows for emotion analyzation by computer technology systems, and has many proposed uses. As Nick D'Alto, the author of this passage, expains "Using video imagery, the new emotion-recognition software tracks these facial movements..." One of the most interesting however, is an emotion curated educational course, using the power of expression to determine and adjust lessons for an individual. As Dr. Huang describes, "A classroom computer could recognize when a student is becoming confused or bored... then it could modify the lesson, like an effective human instructor."

Although Dr. Huang seems to advocate an entirely digital learning experience, this would depend on a school's implementation. For example, this tech could allow for a richer learning experience when the student is not able to attend school, if they are bedridden or if the weather permitted a school closure. Additionally, students could learn whilst on the way back from a vacation, or at home, to help a student understand schoolwork.

Even if schools approached the learning environment autonomously, emotion recognizing tech would allow for a much more fluid learning experience than a self-moderated one.

An argument not presented, but also valid, is that this could allow for virtual assistants, such as Siri or Amazon Alexa, to be given a face, and be able to more effectively "converse" with the user. These assistants could be the heart of a virtual learning experience, to allow for fluid, lifelike teaching and learning, and improve the lives of many students who find themselves confused frequently, and in a position where they cannot easily contact an instructor- a scenerio I often find myself in. Although this technology is a long way from implementation, hopefully schools realize the potential improvements recognizing expressions could allow

in Education, just as projectors, computers, and even electricity have in the past.

Classrooms, as of recently, have been widely criticised as one thing: boring. We've essentially been learning the same way for about 300 years at this point, learning the same way as some of our great great great great grandparents did in colonial times. Though the introduction of more technology into the classroom has helped keep it fresh, the wide consensus is that we don't use the technology that's been given to us enough to make a difference. And, even at that, it doesn't help the fact that students today don't actually learn much going through the American educational system other than how to memorize and spew out information in order to pass a test.

There is a potential solution to this, however. With the new emotion reading technology being developed, Prof. Thomas Whang, from the University of Illinois' Beckman Institute for Advanced Science, stated that using this technology in the classroom could be beneficial; "A classroom computer could recognize when a student is becoming confused or bored... Then it could modify the lesson, like an effective human instructor." Wouldn't it be helpful if there were some way to know if you aren't getting a student's interest in something so that you could teach them more effectively? Or to know beforehand that someone was getting angry, or that something was wrong with how the student was interpreting things?

This is precisely why this technology should be used. Though the whole thing would seem more or less like a giant case study on the American student's emotions, it would be beneficial not only educationally to the students and teachers that way, but it could also possibly benefit students psychologically, too, which could potentially allieviate some of the emotional stress a lot of students have to deal with on a regular basis.

The FACS, or Facial Action Coding System, is a computer program created by Professor Thomas Huang that makes use of various algorithms to detect the emotions of an individual. Although not entirely practical for mordern average home computers, this software has many potential applications. One of such applications is in a classroom setting. Its application in such a setting could prove to be beneficial to students and instructors: it could recognize boredom or confusion in a student and adjust their lesson accordingly, it could detect when a student is not being truthful, and could even potentially help in detecting and treating mental illnesses such as depression and anxiety.

Teaching a lesson to a group of students is not easy, everyone learns best in different ways, some prefer visual aids, and others may prefer hearing the lesson. These are just examples, and in a large group there may be many different types of learners. This presents a challenge to instructors: how can a lesson be structured to best benefit everyone? Unfortunately, it is nearly impossible to create a lesson that allows for everyone to learn it effectively. This is where the FACS could be extremely useful, it could personalize a student's lesson. If a student is learning a lesson and the FACS system detects that said student is confused or bored, as the article mentioned it could, it could adjust that student's lesson to determine what method of teaching works best for that individual and apply it to their lesson. This would allow for much more effective teaching than the traditional method.

Learning is not the only potential application of FACS, though. The article mentions that the system is able to detect subtle facial clues that signal that someone might not be telling the truth, such as detecting if a smile is fake or genuine. It is unfortunate but true that like all people, students sometimes perform unjust or even illegal acts. It is not always easy to determine if a student being questioned for such an act is being entirely truthful. The FACS could detect this, streamlining the process of catching a student guilty of performing such an act. This would allow for much better regulation of behavior and rules in a school or classroom.

Mental illness is not something that is often easy to detect, unlike most physical diseases it does not generally have very obvious physical signs. The article mentions that the FACS has the ability to detect sadness and other related emotions such as anxiousness. Although these are not the sole symptoms of mental illnesses, they are often major parts. If the FACS consistantly detects such emotions in a student, it could alert the school counselor or administrators so that they could ensure the student's wellbeing and provide any help needed.

In summation, Thomas Huang's FACS program could have many potential applications. One of the major applications could be in schools wherein it could be used to help adjust students' lessons to best fit their needs, determine if a student is being truthful, and potentially help detect mental illness in students. If implamented, this system could vastly improve students' overall experience at school and greatly improve their education.

The Facial Action Coding System, or FACS for short, is a new software that is able to read expressions on a person's face and determine that person's emotions based off of the expression. If this technology were equipped in webcams in schools throughout the country, students would have a much better learning experience. The software would be able to sense how a student is reacting to a lesson and would be able to modify it accordingly for the student if needed, as Dr. Huang of the Beckman Institute for Advanced Science at the University of Illinois mentioned. This software could help students stay engaged in their education and increase the overall effectiveness of teaching.

One may argue that students' expressions would not always be read with accuracy, but that is false. The Facial Action Coding System works by tracking all 44 major muscles in the face. The movements of these muscles are closely related to six basic emotions: happiness, surprise, anger, disgust, fear, and sadness. By tracking 44 different muscles, the FACS ensures that it's results are accurate. Dr. Huang previously stated, "The facial expressions for each emotion are universal, even though individuals often show varying degrees of expression." As Dr. Huang explained, even if an individual's expression is not as prominent as another's, it will still be able to be read by the software.

Overall, FACS can be used for many purposes, including school. As aforementioned, FACS would work by changing lessons to better fit a student, based off of their reactions to a lesson. If used in school, FACS will most likely increase the effort put forth by students, the effectiveness of a lesson, and the overall attitude of a community. If a student enjoys the content and the manner in which it is being taught, the effort given by that student will increase. In addition, if students are content with their grades and classes, this feeling of happiness and positivity will most likely pass off onto parents and teachers. In the dawning age of technology upon the rapidly advancing human race, the replacement of a human with a technological innovation has become nearly commonplace. The essence of evolution has been proven to be highly centralized around the concept of making things easier. This innovation does exactly that, but it is questionable as to whether or not it is meeting all of the criteria more sufficiently than a human would. Although computers have reached a point of heavy advancement, no machine could take into account the myriad of variables that find themselves associated with human behavior, and for that reason, they should not be relied upon in an educational environment.

Firstly, it is important to define the problem and its components in this specific context. An emotion is, in its most basic form, an expression of a reaction to a stimulus. The problem lies not within the detection of emotions, but within the unlimited possibilities of these stimuli. Dr. Eckman separated these reactions into the six categories of "happiness, surprise, anger, disgust, fear, and sadness," but he cannot possibly classify all of the derivatives of these reactions. In an educational environment, it is extremely important for a teacher to always understand the situation. Dr. Huang's only claim on this topic is that "a classroom computer could recognize when a student is becoming confused or bored," but that does not even take into account all of the emotions that a student could display, let alone all of the stimuli that could be causing it. A student could be confused or bored simply because the material is going over their head, or perhaps their minds are convoluted as a result of mourning over the loss of a loved one. The software is programmed to analyze the "action units" made by muscular movement, but that muscular movement is simply a reaction to something that cannot be accurately predicted or observed, at least not merely through a countenance. Perhaps this computer can accurately collect data on basic emotion, but it is not going to know what to do with the data it collects if it cannot detect specifically what is causing a specific, undesirable result.

Secondly, it is important to consider the limitations of both humans and machines in this context, and weigh the outcomes accordingly. The author of the article states in the fifth paragraph that "we humans perform this same impressive 'calculation' every day." Such is proven to be true, and so the encouragement for a device to do it for us is asinine. Machines are made for efficiency, and so this concept must be evaluated on the change in efficiency. Clearly, based on the afore point on the impossibility of detection of stimuli, there is a limit to the efficiency of the machine with which the limit to the human efficiency must be compared. In order to solve the blockade between the sender and recipient, the recipient must ascertain to the sender that no harm is done in yielding more information, and the sender must, in turn, yield more information. Human interpersonal exchange executes this procedure perfectly, but based on the article alone, Huang's software cannot serve as a sufficient sender, nor a sufficient recipient, for it can neither ask for more information nor interpret information that it gets. A teacher can make the same observational interpretation by reading their students' faces, but the difference is that a teacher can ask what is troubling them and offer support, for it is the stimulus that is causing the problem to arise, for without a stimulus, there is no physical or emotional reaction. "Most human communication is nonverbal, including emotional communication," admits Dr. Huang. Therefore, this emotional communication should not be treated as something so formulaic; as something that is easily decipherable by anything simpler than the infinitely diverse and complex human brain.

Dr. Huang's creation is undoubtedly impressive, and will serve an effective purpose somewhere in the world, but that purpose does not reside in an academic environment. Its properties are accurate, but it lacks the psychological ability to help a student, or a person in general, tackle a problem in the way that it is needed to be handled. This software may be able to accurately observe for humans, but until it can accurately think for them, and communicate for them, and resolve for them, it is the job of none other than the human to make sure that something is being done about any problems that they encounter. Humans are not algorithmic creatures, and no algorithmic software is ever going to provide them with the emotional nor psychological support that they need in order for them to move forward.

In the article "Making Mona Lisa Smile.", Nick D'Alto writes about a new computer technology called the Facial Action Coding System (FACS). This system enables the computer on which it is downloaded to read the emotions of the human that is using it. One major use of this technology that D'Alto writes about, can be in the classroom. This technology can indeed be a very useful tool for students, teachers, and parents alike.

"A classroom computer could recognize when a student is becoming confused or bored," says Dr. Huang, one of the founding professors that is working on developing this product. "Then it could modify the lesson, like an effective human instructor." If this is true, it could change classrooms forever. Say, for example, a struggling student is having trouble understanding his biology homework, while the student next to him is doing just fine. With this new technology, the struggling student would be able to access additional example problems or lessons that would be generated by the computer program, and this would all happen while the other student is continuing on with the lesson.

Not only can this new technology be useful for students, but it can also be beneficial to the teachers as well. If this new technology could aid students without them even asking for help, the teacher would not have to worry about which students are understanding the lesson and which ones are not. Additionally, the teacher wouldn't have to interrupt their class time to help a struggling student. Teachers also would not have to worry about the students hiding their struggling academic situation either. Humans (including teachers) are vulnerable to deception via false facial expressions. For example, if the biology teacher of the student previously mentioned were to ask him if he needed help with the lesson, that student might lie and tell the teacher, "No, I'm ok," followed by a false smile on his face. The teacher would then walk on, not knowing that the student was actally feeling miserable about what he was learning. This problem could be fixed by the Facial Action Coding System. D'Alto explains in paragraphs 4, 7, and 8 that the new technology would be able to detect the false emotions displayed by the human user. Dr. Huang says that, "Most human communication is nonverbal... so computers need to understand that, too." Therefore, this new system would eliminate the need for teachers to pry a student open in order for them to ask for help.

Furthermore, this useful technology would eliminate the need for parent intervention in a student's education. Much like the ability to replace a teacher's aid, the new system would be able to help students at any time that they are struggling. Therefore, parents would not have to worry about helping their children to succeed in academic areas. The Facial Action Coding System would be able to help the students while they finish their homework at home too.

Overall, the Facial Action Coding System would be a very valuable addition to the classroom. The students would benefit from the additional help, without having to ask for it. The teachers and parents would benefit from the relief of stress. The new technology would definitely be a very helpful utility for all who would be affected by it.

full_text:
When a teacher plans out their lesson, may be thinking of practicality and logic. They may be thinking about their pre-planned syllabus. What they may not be thinking about, however, is the students' ability to grasp every concept they teach. And when it comes time for the students to test on the information they've "learned", the teacher soon finds out via test scores that the lesson may not have been grasped as easily as they thought. Using the Facial Action Coding System, teachers could analyze the faces of the students to detect confusion and work their lesson plan around to make what they're teaching easier to understand. Perhaps they could even put a smile on the students' faces! That is why the facial recognition technology would be valuable in classrooms.

The Facial Action Coding system is a computer algorithm designed to detect the use of different facial muscles to determine a person's emotions. It begins by forming a computerized 3-D model of the person's face. It analyzes all 44 muscles in a human face, detecting the movement of one as an "action unit". Then, it analyzes six different basic emotions: happiness, fear, anger, disgust, sadness, and surprise. Using these basic emotions, as well as the movement of certain muscles in the person's face, the FACS can determine which emotion the person is feeling.

This wonder of technology would be very useful in determining the emotions of students. As Dr. Huang stated, "A classroom computer could recognize when a student is becoming confused or bored." As a result of becoming bored or confused, students may not fully grasp the lesson they are being taught. With FACS, a teacher would know when a student began to become confused or bored. Consequently, they would be able to adjust their lesson plan to make it easier to understand or make what they are teaching less of a boring topic.

Just as well, the FACS could help put smiles on the students' faces. When the lesson is adjusted to make it less of a drawl, it could even become fun. The teacher could add certain things to the lesson to make it fun, especially when they realize that the students aren't really paying attention. According to the Theory of Emotion, "...moving your facial muscles not only expresses emotions, but also may even help produce them." Getting the students to smile, even just for a little while, could help make boredom disappear.

The FACS in the classroom would be a very valuable tool. FACS would help teachers to modify their lessons, thus making them easier to grasp. Especially when teachers are only thinking logically, this would be extermely useful. And when students start to become bored, FACS would help teachers make the lesson fun. Practicality is great, but who wouldn't want learning to be fun as well?

full_text:
Most people have, at some point, seen the Mona Lisa by Leonardo Da Vinci, not necessarily the real one in Paris, but some sort of duplicate. The piece is incredibly iconic with almost anyone in the digital era being able to recognize it at first glance. While Mona Lisa herself may be known for her smile, it could be possible that she's been faking it the entire time. In Nick D'Alto's article about recent facial recognition technology, he discusses the anatomical composition of the Mona Lisa's face, and it is indeed happy. With technology like this, real world situations could become much more convinient due to the ability for technology to immediately recognize our positive or negative reactions to certain things, in particular, student's reactions within classroom settings. Facial recognition technology can provide a much more engaging learning experience for students and is valuable to student's learning experiences as well as teacher's teaching abilities.

With the use of, as it's called, Facial Action Coding Scanner, computers can immediately identify how students feel about particular classroom aspects and activities. This creates an opportunity for teachers to edit and maximize the learning experience for students. It would also allow teachers to prescribe certain assignments to students who feel especially disconnected by providing extra assistance, or especially excited by getting them more involved with the material beyond that which is tought in a textbook. As Dr Huang says in the article: "A classroom computer could recognize when a student is becoming confused or bored." Based off of how the collective students feel about a particular topic or activity, the teacher could manipulate how they approach that topic or abort the activity if it is far too ineffective for classroom use. If students feel disengaged and become less interested in a topic as a result of the activity, it is vital that it be abandoned. This will allow students to stay engaged by providing them with assignments that pique their interest rather than damage their passion for a topic.

Beyond elementary use, FACS can develop a realistic model of the human face with almost any emotion using all 44 muscles in the face. This type of technology could be crucial for multiple types of courses across student's school careers. People in classes discussing sociology could identify the relationship between speech and facial features, such as how positive comments trigger muscles that imply happiness or lack thereof in the case of an impairment. Another critical use could be for children with underdeveloped social skills who are unable to immediately identify other's emotions like most children can. This is an extreme disability since, as Dr Huang says, "Most human communication is nonverbal, including emotional communication, so computers need to understand that, too." Children could learn to identify how the use of certain muscle's in other's faces symbolize certain emotions and other nonverbal communications such as pain or pleasure.

A valid response to the article could be to identify when the author talks about empathy and claims, "(Empathy) may happen because we unconsciously imitate another person's facial expressions." This evidence supports the idea that teachers themselves can identify the reactions of students to certain classroom settings and makes the computer-generated facial recognition software completely superfluous. Despite this, however, students can feel complex emotions, especially during transitional years, where emotions can be more difficult to recognize, even by psychology teachers. We can see this when the author describes the Mona Lisa's emotions at the beginning and says, "She's 83 percent happy, 9 percent disgusted, 6 percent fearful, and 2 percent angry." It is not readily apparent to one looking at the Mona Lisa that she is fearful, and, in the same way, it is not readily apparent to a teacher or counselor

if a student is completely uninterested. For situations like these, computers are able to identify anatomically when students feel certain emotions, rather than relying on the often inaccurate instincts of teachers.

A good teacher can get his students to memorize something, then repeat it on a test, but it takes far more effort to get one's students legitimately excited about topics even when the material has very little interest value. In order to maximize each students interest in a classroom setting, it's vital to understand how one's students feel about what one says or does. Since this cannot and should not be solely assessed by teachers, computer facial recognition is the path to success. By being able to help socially impaired children and engage students in concepts, the case for using FACS in the classroom is strong, not just for students but for our nation as a whole. Many refer to the youth of today as the future of America, and in order to have a bright future, schools ought to brighten our youth with passion. A bright student does not simply memorize information, they cherish it, they keep it, and they use it for their country to drive itself towards a better tomorrow.

In addition to the purpose of the program, there needs to be thought about the attention that a school administration would pay tosuch a program. This can get tricky because a school system has so many areas of interest to maintain, and a computer system such as Dr. Huang's would raise the cost in dollars. It is hard to say if the system would make the adequate adjustments needed to preserve the privacy of the students from an academic standpoint, which would involve the emotions they feel about school, school life, or the academic habits at home.

The Facial Action Coding System is an undeniably amazing invention. A machine that can detect human emotions via even the slightest of facial movements could have very promising future results in fields such as criminal and political investigation, as well as settings such as that of a therapist. However, this is not a technology that needs to be within the schooling system. There would be little to no use for this technology within the classroom, the data could be unreliable or misleading, dangerous to some students, and it could very well remove the human element of communicaiton between students and even teachers.

First, we can start with the extremely limited use for this technology within the regular classroom. One major issue seen from the start is that for this technology to be implemented school-wide, schools would need to be able to provide computers to all students and computers. While some schools may be able to afford that, others simply cannot. Then there is the issue of use past the novelty of it within class. The only real cases where this could be used as a learning tool are when students are looking into psycology or criminal investigation. In these cases, yes, it could be a valueable tool in helping students get a head start on reading facial features to find the truth. However these are ever-increasingly rare examples, with many students today not showing very much interest in these fields.

Secondly, trying to use this to tell the emotions of every student could be unreliable or even minorly dangerous to students. The many different facial features of humans today can create an enormously wide range of expressions to mean different things. This opens up possiblity for the machine to mistake certain looks for emotions that aren't really there, creating a false report. Everybody knowing the emotions of others could also be a gateway to possibly increased bullying in schools. While it would be a nice belief that students want to help one another, especially when one is upset or sad, that simply isn't the world we live in today. Students still bully those below them and those that have things like times of major sadness or anger. If another student can always see this, it can create a target for the student who is upset or sad, furthering the unhealthy state via the other student bullying them and/or pushing towards more intense versions of these feelings.

Additionally, a student may not necessarily want others to know what they are feeling all of the time. Students have a wide array of different home situations in which different events may be happening to cause many different emotions. However many times a student doesn't like to disclose this information, and would rather deal with it on their own accord. While it is nice to offer help to others that are feeling ways other than mostly happy, some students become more upset or unstable when this is done. Some simply need to work through things on their own and with those close to them, not everyone around them.

Lastly, but most importantly, this could be removing the human element of in-person communication. It is part of being human to read other's emotions and help when you can. Having a machine tell you when someone is upset or angry or disgusted would just make this offering impersonal. If you offer help to someone only after having the program read their emotions, it creates less sympathy and more of an automated response, effectively making the human act as a program as well. True care towards another human should come from the heart, not the machine saying you should care. The article states that "we humans perfom this same impressive 'calculation' every day.", and goes on to say that you can most likely tell how a friend is feeling by looking at their face. As students, it is important to be able to learn to read features like this and their meanings when they are younger to have for the rest of their lives rather than relying on a machine to make the correct calculations for them. The article also states a quote from Dr. Huang: "Most human communication is nonverbal, including emotional communication. So computers need to understand that, too." In all fairness, I do believe Dr. Huang is right about this. It can be massively important in certain respects for the machine to be able to know how a person is feeling and whether they are telling the truth. However a person using this to find the emotions of another while in a classroom is simply unnecessary.

In all, the program is not a bad idea or invention, not in the slightest. It shows great promise and can be of use to those within fields where finding a lie is of great importance. In terms of schooling however, it has a higher chance of doing more harm than good. It would have little to no use in the classroom itself, it could give false information on how students are feeling, encourage bullying and isolation of certain students, and it could remove the learned human element of communication from this young age. It is a case of a fascinating technology, but an unneeded one for standard schooling.

FACS is not a valuable tool in the classroom simply because it is not accurate enough to calculate emotions with any degree of certainty. Researchers who invented FACS broke down the muscles in the face attempted to determine which muscles were used when certain emotions were present. However, many of these criteria were very broad; researchers inputted one sign of anger as when "your orbicularis oris (around your mouth) tightens your lips to show anger." This kind of generalization may work sometimes, but since everyone, and especially young students in classrooms (or in a more specific case, students with facial deformities or paralysis) show emotions with slightly different muscles, this general look at the facial muscle groups will not suffice. Everyone has a different smile.

In addition, this technology is not valuable in schools because of the rather general look at emotion is broken down into distinctly negative categories. As explained in the text, the psycologist Dr. Paul Eckman "classified six basic emotions- happiness, surprise, anger, disgust, fear, and sadness- and then associated each with characteristic movements of the facial muscles" showing that five out of the six basic emotions were neutral or negative. Along with not showing base emotions that may not fit the six, students in classrooms all express emotion differently. If the program is has higher numbers of negative emotional categories, it is statistically more likely to assign some percentage of a students face to a negative category. In addition to this not being accurate, teachers may make unneeded adjustments to the student's lessons based on small percentages that the student may or may not feel.

Finally, the program loses its valuable function in schools because of natural human tendencies and flaws that could cause the computer to interpret students inaccurately. The article talks about future viablility of the program in advertising stating that "if you smile when a Web ad appears on your screen, a similar ad might follow. But if you frown, the next ad will be different." This demonstrates the ignorance of the program of human tendencies and differences. While one person may smile at a funny or heartwarming ad, another person may have had a bad day and merely wants to get rid of the ad as fast as possible, causing them to frown at an ad they would normally have found enjoyable. In addition, there are human emotions the could be hard to place in any cateory, such as concern, passive aggression, and confusion. This is a special case with young students, who are still developing their own distinct personalities; the software may lose some of these small details and misinterpret what a student needs, thus making it unfit for use in classrooms.

Although the FACS program could be a valuable tool to some industries, one it should not be implimented in is school systems with students. FACS would not be a valuable tool because of its low accuracy with broad generalizations, its mostly negative emotional categories, and its failure to pick up on subtle human flaws. It is the twenty-first century and driverless cars are finally becoming a reality. They are constantly gaining more media coverage by the day. However, do we really require the development of these driverless cars? The answer is quite simple and rather obvious. No, we do not need driverless cars for a numerous amount of reasons.

Despite all the positive aspects being publicized of these driverless cars, there are plethora of overshadowed negative aspects that go with it. Besides, humanity is very much capable of driving their own cars. Google cofounder Sergey Brin firmly believes that the world will thrive under the introduction of these driverless cars. What about the costs? Surely it will cost millions to produce the technology required to operate these cars. Also, the consumers will have to pay more money to purchase them from the companies. If cost was not a major issue alone, safety most defintitely is.

Cars are constantly being regulated and tested for safety. Are these driverless cars really safe though? The goal of the production of these cars is to allow the driver more freedom. However, a driver is still required to be behind the wheel and take over in certain instances. If the driver is preoccupied because they are under the assumption that the car will be doing all the driving for them, it could lead to an accident under the circumstances in which the driver actually does need to assume control over their automobile. That is not the end of it's safety problems though. Google has stated that "Their cars have driven more than half a million miles without a crash". They fail to mention whether or not it was a closed course in which the car was driven. If they are using these statistics that have only been collected since 2009, it is hard to rely soley on that data considering driver operated cars have been used for a much longer time period, and have been driven numerous distances farther than half a million miles.

Let it not be forgotten that these are "driverless cars". Their name implies that no driver is required, when in fact a driver must still be present behind the wheel at all times. The name itself contradicts the point it is trying to make. Now when driving, distractions are certainly a problem for all drivers. Some may argue that by not having to drive they will not have to worry about being distracted. If the drivers become so accustomed to being able to forward their attention towards their "distractions" instead of driving, it is likely they could miss a notification or alert sent by the car that requires their control because they are simply too accustomed to not having to drive.

The technology created for these driverless cars is almost certainly likely to malfunction at one point or another. When it does, accidents can and will occur. Now, not only is there the dilemna of an accident that has to be dealt with, there is also the question of whether the driver is liable or the manufacter of the driverless cars. With the introduction of these driverless cars and the risks that come with their potentially faulty technology, lawsuits are sure to trail. Since the driverless cars still in their early stages of development, many car manufacturers may be wary to start production.

The negative aspects of the production of driverless cars are infinite. For the greater good, it is wisest to not waste the time, effort, and resources that would be needed to create these cars.

Driverless cars have been in development in some form since the 1950s, when General Motors created a car that could run by itself on a specific test track (3). However, driverless cars on regular motorways began to be practical just recently. Google has specifically been working on driverless cars in these conditions since 2009 and these cars have driven over 500,000 miles without crashing (2). However, their cars aren't fully driverless; when something out of the ordinary happens while driving, the car alerts the driver to take over. Even so, driverless cars are starting to be thought of as viable alternatives to traditional automobiles.

There are some setbacks within the idea of a driverless car. As aforementioned, most cars in development that are "driverless" still need human drivers behind the wheel to take over if road conditions become unusual. Also, the development of these cars requires much more funding to equip each car with the sensors it needs to effectively mimic human driving skills. In the modified Toyota Prius made by Google, the sensors needed included "position-estimating sensors on the left rear wheel, a rotating sensor on the roof, a video camera mounted near the rearview mirror, four automotive radar sensors, a GPS receiver, and an inertial motion sensor" (4). This would force car manufacturers to spend much more money so that these driverless cars would be fully functional. However, technology in this day and age is extremely advanced, much more so than in the 50s with the first attempt at driverless car manufacturing. This advancement in technology makes it much easier for today's car manufacturers to start implementing driverless technology in their cars. In driverless cars, there is also the issue of fault in accidents (9). While Google's aforementioned cars have driven over 500,000 miles without crashing, there is always the chance of technological failure. If a driverless car gets in an accident with a normal automobile, there could be very heated conflicts and lawsuits involving the two drivers and the manufacturer of the driverless car. However, the benefits involved with driverless cars outweigh the setbacks.

One major benefit involved with driverless cars is the fact that driverless cars effectively eliminate human error, specifically drunk driving. Thousands of people are killed or injured every year by drunk or intoxicated drivers. Also, if no accident occurs, the drunk or intoxicated drivers operating these vehicles are sometimes pulled over and arrested by law enforcement. A relatively new app called Uber allows a smartphone user to contact an Uber driver to pick them up and take them to their destination. It is effectively a personalized taxi service. Uber is used very frequently by drunk or intoxicated people that otherwise would not have a way to get from place to place, eliminating the hazards to the general public of drunk driving. Driverless cars would helps eliminated accidents involving drivers who are drunk or intoxicated in the same way that Uber does. Another major benefit of driverless cars is that if driverless cars were used in public transportation, these services would be benefitted greatly and help many more people. One of Google's cofounders, Sergey Brin, envisions a future of public transportation using driverless cars as a fleet of public-transport taxis. These cars, or at least the ones he envisions would use half the fuel of the taxis used today and would be far more flexible and personal than the buses used today (1). This driverless taxi system offers a far better alternative to both today's taxi system and today's bus system.

Driverless cars are becoming a major innovation in both the automotive and technological industry. While there are some potential setbacks involved with the development of these vehicles, driverless cars effectively reduce and/or eliminate human error from roadways and offer a viable alternative to bus services, taxi services, and drunk drivers.

Everyone today seems to be obsessed with things we only dreamed of 10 or so years ago. With hoverboards and Siri available to us, things of the future seem more appealing and possible now. The sky is the limit. But just because we can create something, does that mean we should? The idea of driverless cars has been around for a long time, and some versions have actually already been made. Cars that can drive themselves have fascinated people through movies and television. But now that driverless cars are almost here, should they be put to use? Everyone seems to share the same goal of making life easier, better, and more enjoyable. The advances we have had and are making in science, technology, etc. are pursuing these same goals. Thus one has to ask; would driverless cars really make life that much better for us? Most likely not.

There are many positive and negative aspects of driverless cars, as there is with every new invention. However, the negative aspects outweigh the positive ones, at least for the cars that manufacturers are planning to create now. One major negative aspect of the driverless cars now is that they aren't truly driverless. For example, the article "Driverless Cars Are Coming" explained that Google cars still "alert the driver to take over when pulling in and out of driveways or dealing with complicated traffic issues, such as navigating through roadwork or accidents". This seems to take away from the appeal of the driverless car. If the human driver will need to take control over the car at times, that means they always have to be alert. This shows that driverless cars would not really make traveling easier for the driver. The article points out that "manufactuers are also considering using cameras to watch that drivers are remaining focused on the road. While the driver watches the road, the car watches the driver". This additional feature on the driverless car adds unneeded complications. It would also prove more difficult to get and keep the driver's attention if they don't have to drive most of the time. Driverless cars aren't truly driverless and add more complexity and management to assure that drivers are ready to take over when they need to.

Another negative aspect of driverless cars deals with entertainment and the driver's enjoyment. Although it seems very easy and stress free to travel by driverless car, there is a question about who would want to have a driverless car that still needs a driver. Won't drivers get bored waiting for their turn to drive? It turns out that manufactuers have already taken this into account. Because people tend to get bored easily, most people need entertainment. The article brings up that "some manufacturers hope to do that (driving fun in a new way) by bringing in-car entertainment and information systems that use heads-up displays. Such displays can be turned off instantly when the driver needs to take over". While this idea covers the safety aspect of in-car entertainment, it is overly complex and would most likely cost a lot of money. Instead of having the driver being "entertained" and fully engaged by the actions of driving, driverless cars would have to make up for the lack of entertainment with expensive and complicated technology and would have to assure that the driver is alert with even more technology. It seems to be more of a hassle than a luxury.

Although driverless cars could potentially make transportation easier and reduce our use of fuel in the future, right now they are not a good investment. The idea alone allures many people to this invention, but driverless cars will not prove to be as benefitical to us, at least in this time period. Many argue that driverless cars would increase safety on our roads, but this is not completely true. In order for driverless cars to truly be safe, the driver still needs to be fully attentive to the road and ready to take over. However, this will most likely not be the case, since there is a lack motivation for the driver to stay alert. Driverless cars would also require unneccessary technology to keep the idle driver entertained. Overall, driverless cars would not benefit our lives enough to invest a lot in this field. Though driverless cars might not be what we are looking for, there are still many other areas to research and invest in, in order to improve the lives of everbody.

While driverless cars are a wonderful idea and would be an amazing advancement in technology, it is unnecessary to continue to develop driverless cars at this time. They might make more sense in the future, but people are doing fine with regular cars and the way driving is now, so there is no reason to try to continue to develop the cars at this point. Developers should wait until there is some sort of need for driverless cars.

In theory, driverless cars are great, but driverless cars are not completely driverless. This completely defeats the purpose of a driverless car. If there is a person driving or waiting to drive, it is no longer driverless. There will always need to be a driver in the car, so why devote so much time, energy, and money to something that, at this point, will not even give that much of a benefit? There is no need for driverless cars if people are still going to have to be in the driver's seat paying attention to the road. This defeats the purpose of a driverless car.

It costs a lot of money to continue development on these cars, and even more money to buy one. This is money that could be spent elsewhere on more pressing needs in the world. Driverless cars are not of high importance in society's wants and needs. If developments continue to be made and there continues to be more research, then there will be a lot of money spent on the research aspect, and if nobody wants to buy one of these cars, that is a lot of money wasted on research that will not be made back if the cars do not sell.

It is also a matter of whether the people want them or not. People are content with the ways cars are now. They see no need for driverless cars, so they will not buy them, and the few people that do buy them will be the minority on the roads. This is the exact scenario where the driverless car becomes no longer driverless. If there are other people on the roads in normal cars, and the sensors in the driverless car can only do so much, there will need to be a driver anyway in the driverless car. If there is still a driver in the car, why spend the extra money on a driverless car instead of just getting a regular car? It defeats the purpose of the driverless car if someone still has to drive it. People will not see a need for these cars, so they will not buy them, and if nobody is going to buy them, they should not continue work on the project. It is pointless to continue progress on a project that will never get off the ground.

In theory, driverless cars would be a huge advancement in technology, but there is simply no need for them right now. People would not benefit from them at this point. People are perfectly content with the way cars are now and have no pressing desire to switch to a driverless car. There would be lots of wasted time, energy, and money that could have been spent elsewhere. They may become helpful and more practical in the future, but for now, driverless cars should be put on the shelf and saved for a later date when it becomes more reasonable to use them.

A sudden surge in the use of technology has pushed humanity forward in technological advances and innovations. The idea of Driverless Cars are becoming a topic of more and more discussion and experimentation. The question, however, is not only when the Driverless Cars will be ready, but should they be put to use? The answer to that is "no".

Though Driverless Cars have not been fully developed yet, the prospect of them being on the roads is daunting. Ther positive aspects of a driverless cars are that they use half the fuel of today's taxis and offer more flexibility than a bus. That, however, is about where the positives stop.

So far, modern technology has been able to develop a driverless car that can drive 25 miles per hour on its own, though it is not completely driverless. The driverless cars are able to navigate through easy driving situations, however, if it were to come to an accident, or contruction, the driver would have to maually take over. That leaves a lot of room for extra things that need to be worked out. One of those things being how a driver is notified to take over. Several ways have been developed, a few being that the driver's seat vibrates, the car tells the driver to take over, or all the displays in the car (for things lie texting, calling, etc.) will be turned off to notify the driver to pay attention to the road. But how much time would be needed to notify the driver of a potential accident?

Other ideas have consisted of upgrading roads, however this costs a lot of money to install all upgrades and would instill too much reliabilty on technology. A solution to this was to make completly driverless cars, though that too would require enormous amounts of upgrades and money. Cars would need a constant 3D scan of the surrounding area to know where it was that other cars were, streets were signs were, and buildings were to name a few things. This is not only expensive but offers too much opportunity for error.

Having an all technology, automated car would also open cars up to a greater chance for tampering with cars, altering cars, or theft.

Following all the doubts about automated cars, money, upgrades, there are still many unanswered questions, which would only be the beginning in addition to the confusion of consumers. Who has to buy the cars? Everyone? How much would they cost... to buy? To produce? What is the likelihood of a malfunction? How would the cars be repaired? Who would make the cars? Who is responsible for accidents that may occur? How would people be trained/taught to use these cars? Why do we even need automated cars?

A sudden surge in the use of technology has pushed humanity forward in technological advances and innovations but in light of new inventions, the reliability on technology will become overwhelming. Driverless cars should not be put to use due to the many uncertainties, opportunities for error, public confusion, the need for new laws, and all the unanswered questions that pose a threat to the safety of the public.

Driverless cars are a great new technological advancement and may offer many benefits, but they are not pratical. Google cofounder Sergey Brin envisions driverless cars that will use half of the fuel of today's taxis and will change the world. However, driverless cars are simply too impractical to be efficitent.

As of 2016, no 'driverless cars' are completely driverless. BMW announced the development of a car that can steer, accelerate, and brake themselves, but human assistance is required in work zones, accidents, etc. There are psychological aspects that need to be evaluated in automation. The technology that is being used right now still needs human assistance at certian times so the driver must always stay alert. This may cause problems due to the fact that people might assume that they can take a break from driving because it's a driverless car. This can cause dangerous accidents if the driver does not take control of the car when they need to.

The amount of technology and equipment needed to make many cars driverless is impractical for world-wide use. Google's modified Toyota Prius uses many sensors including position-estimating sensors on the left rear wheel, a rotating sensor on the roof, a video camera near the rearview mirror, four automotive radar sensors, an inertial motion sensor, and a GPS reciever. All of these input mechanics help driverless cars mimic the skill of a human driver, but even with this much equipment no cars are completely driverless. Some companies like Nissan plan to have cars that can drive themselves by 2020. Think of all the other sensors that will be needed on complelety driverless cars to be safe for public use. The sensors will have to be able to mimic human skill a lot more and more sensors will most likely have to be manufactured and tested. The cost of driverless cars is also a factor that makes them impractible. The money for the sensors alone will be very high and then the car itself will have to be added on to that. Too much money will be spent on something that can be really dangerous for everyone on the road.

In most states is it illegal to even test driverless cars. There are too many safety hazards and accidents waiting to happen for driverless cars right now to be in full use. Even with all of the sensors completely driverless cars may have, how do we know that one of those cars won't completely malfunction? If one of the cars malfunctions on an interstate the effects can be catastrophic, especially of there are a mix of driverless and not driverless cars on the road. Some driverless cars might see the accident but they won't be able to alert the driver quick enough for the driver to take action. Maybe the car will try to suddenly stop on its own which might cause more wrecks because of the high speed of travel. The safety issues are simply too great for driverless cars to be used world-wide.

Driverless cars may be the next big technological achievement, but as of right now, smarter cars are simply too money-consuming, human relying, and unsafe to be in use. The cars being tested now still need a lot of human assistance and the amount of technology that will keep the amount of human assistance down will be very expensive. The cars will be too unsafe to use and that is why they are impractible.

Driverless cars are something people have always watched in movies and dreamed about having ourselves. Now it seems like driverless cars could be a possibility. And while that's exciting, we have to ask ourselves, is it worth it? There is positive things about having driverless cars, there is no doubting that. But there is also negative things that could conteract the positive, and we have to carefully observe the pros and cons.

The article, Driverless Cars are coming, starts out by saying these cars would use half the fuel of today's taxis and offer far more flexibility than buses. That is obviously a reason driverless cars are a good idea. We won't always have all the fuel needed to keep our cars running and as a result it is quite expensive which makes fuel unpractical for some people, even though they may need it. Also, busses are a hassel, therefore, so far driverless cars seem like a good idea. But are they really?

Even though Google has had cars that can drive under specific conditions and have driven more than half a million miles without a crash, they still aren't completely driverless. This is where we run into our first problem. The car will alert the driver to take over when dealing with something such as complicated traffic. Well that all sounds fine until you really think about it.

I know it can already sometimes be hard to stay awake at the wheel, even if it's only for a short amount of time because sometimes, we are just tired. And if we don't have the respnsibility of keeping the car on the road, whose to say we won't fall asleep? It already happens, even without driverless cars. If you fall asleep at the wheel of this car and suddenly the car needs you to take over, there may be a problem. Even though you might wake up, you may not be able to comprehend what is happening yet. And it only takes a few seconds to crash.

Then in 2013, BMW announced the development of Traffic Jam Assistant. Sounds good right? Well yeah, but again we have the problem of the driver staying alert. This car can steer, accelerate, and brake themselves just like other driverless cars we've heard about. And this car has special touch sensors to make sure the driver keeps ahold of the wheel. But even if the driver keeps ahold of the wheel, whose to say they couldn't still dooze off? Besides, this car can only handle driving functions at speeds 25 mph or lower. I know I don't know a lot about driving, but I do know there are places where that is just too slow.

Now, I have to admit there is a lot of options to making sure the driver stays alert. One of them is to keep the driver occupied. Some manufacturers are hoping to bring in-car entertainment to the car. So maybe something like a movie or show to keep you busy. To me, that does sound like a good idea.

There are also many different ways to alert the driver that the car needs to be taken over. Those ways include flashing lights on the windshield, a vibrating drivers seat and more. Also, another idea is using a camera to watch that drivers are remaining focused on the road. These are all good ideas but still may not be completly foolproof.

Like I said in the begining, there are some positives to having a driverless car. Do these positives outweigh the negatives? That I don't know yet. But we do need to look at both sides.

Two positives that I already mentioned are of course reduced need for fuel and less hassel than taking a public bus. Another postive aspect of this is that the information from sensors that would be on the car can cause the car to apply brakes on individual wheels and reduce power from the engine. That in turn allows far better response and control than a human driver could manage alone.

And, futher improvements in sensors to make driving safer are also leading to cars that can handle more driving tasks on their own which in my opinion, is very important.

So in conclusion, do I think driverless cars are a good idea? Well, yes, I think that it could be a very positive thing for our future. But, there needs to be a lot more improvements before driverless cars are our reality.

Right now, driverless cars aren't even allowed to be tested in most states and I think that proves that they are dangerous. There is just to many risks involved. Besides the obvious risk of crashing, we have the problem of who is to blame in an accident? The driver or the manufacture? I can already see that causing problems.

So, while I do think driverless cars are a great idea and could be a really amazing thing, I don't think they are ready yet. I want them to be a lot safer before they are released to the public. That being said, as of right now, I don't think driverless cars are a good idea. They just aren't safe enough yet.

An example would be that those driverless cars only assist the driver, so they still need a person ready to react if the car needs help in specific situations, which eliminates the core virtue of the car being driverless. Another is that if there were to be an accident caused by a driverless car that is still drivable by man, who would be the one to blame for it? But, there still is no true evidence of a car being completely efficient on its' own. As stated within the article, "None of the cars developed so far are completely driverless. They can steer, accelerate, and brake themselves but all are designed to notify the driver when the road ahead requires human skills" (7). There are still features missing within a car that don't allow it to be fully functional on its' own; it can perform basic commands, but cannot do other functions that are seen on the road. All cars still require "human skills" which means that the driverless car, isn't completely driverless in the first place. This is negative because if a consumer wants a car to drive itself, why would he/she still have to be fully alert just in case something happens to where the car can't do it on its' own? It completely defeats the purpose of the car being driverless if it cannot do these tasks alone. This is one major negative aspect of the development of driverless cars because it cannot provide the services wanted by the people in our world today. But this isn't the only issue given through the idea of driverless cars, safety seems to be a major concern for most people.

Cars that are able to drive themselves are still a negative proposal because of the safety concerns regarding regulations and accidents on roads. If there isn't anyone able to keep watch of the car, than that entity on the road is not allowed in the first place. This article states, "Presently, traffic laws are written with the assumption that the only safe car has a human driver in control at all times...If the technology fails and someone is injured, who is at fault - the driver or the manufacturer?" (9). Only a vehicle on the road that contains an alert and awake driver is considered to be safe according to numerous traffic laws. So what this means is that if there is no person within the vehicle controlling it with their own hands, that entity should not be allowed on the road.
