And without a singular person driving the car, than that vehicle is considered unsafe, which shows how this can negatively affect the complete safety of those on or around the road.

Overall, the creation of driverless cars is having a major negative impact on the world as a whole by not being fully functional and pushing forth safety concerns for all people on the roads. Through the recent development of driverless cars, there are features missing from them that would consider them driverless in the first place. They are only allowed to steer, accelerate, and brake which would enforce major safety concerns on those in or around them. If there is no driver in control of the vehicle, than there is no telling what would happen if an accident occurred, and who should cover the expenses for it. Speeding into the Future

Everyone wants to have the latest and greatest technology. Recent developments in the field of science has allowed the rapid introduction of new inventions. Those inventions are produced and introduced into the market quickly. These new creations are designed to make human life easier. The development of driverless cars should not continue. It should not contunue because there are legal issues that have yet to be discussed, the prices of cars increase, and computers cannot do everything that humans can do.

The first red light is the issue of all the legal battles that would come with self driving cars. Few driverless cars are on the roads. There would have to be more testing to see if they work better than those driven by humans. The issues that would need to be solved include who would be at fault in an accident. If a person is not in control of the car, they should not be liable for the accident. However, the automaker also really isn't at fault since the consumer bought the vehicle at their own risk. It would be a never ending blame game. Some may believe that changing the laws would be easy. However, this is a complex issue and would take years. The US government looks into both sides of issues extensively, but the opposing parties would make it close to impossible for anything to pass. The government should spend time worrying about more serious issues such as diplomatic relations and solving the social issues of the American people. Driverless cars are a distraction and should not continue to be developed.

In addition to the red lights of legal battles, there are detours surrounding the price issue. These cars will lead to an increase in the price of vehicles. All the sensors, global position systems (GPS), radars, and cameras will raise the already skyhigh prices even higher. The average car payment in the US per month is over $400. Average new car prices are well over $20,000. With the new technology, those prices will go up. Adding expensive technology will raise the overall price. Some economists and technological enthusiasts would argue that the prices of all the gadgets have gone down-radar was once two million dollars. However, the multitude of devices on the new cars would still add up to a ton. Car insurance would also go up because of the new risks on the road, as well as the fact that cars will go up. The money that will potentially be charged to the consumers is best spent elsewhere.

The last major roadblock for the journey of driverless cars is that computers cannot do everything that humans can do. In the article, it states that drivers still have to take over when the circumstances are too difficult for computers to handle, such as heavy traffic, backing up, or construction zones. If this is true, can a computerized car be trusted completey to get a person from the starting point to the destination safely? Opponents would argue that car crashes kill thousands of people every year in the United States. They would say that self-driving cars could lower that number. However, heavy traffic, backing up, and construction zones are not that difficult. If the driverless cars cannot do those simple tasks, then investing time and money will not make driving any safer.

In conclusion, driverless cars should no longer be under construction. Their development should be stalled. There are too many legal issues to manuver, the prices of cars would increase, and computers cannot do everything that humans can do. So, instead of speeding into the future with driverless cars, let us carefully cruise into what science has in store.

Not only are ther distractions inside the car but there are numerous distractions from outside the car that could lead to hindering the driver. Lastly the fact that the car is run primarily by sensors and and video cameras could lead to many problems that the driver would have no control over. Machinery is not always reliable and if a sensor or the GPS broke or malfunctioned it could lead to a car crash and possible injuries of passengers. The development of these cars shouldn't be continued until safe solutions have been found to deal with these dangers and make driverless cars safe to manufacture and use.

Although driverless cars are very dangerous they can also be exceedingly expensive. Manufacturing an entirely new type of car would lead to the expense of the the new technology and parts required to build the cars. Not only that but once the cars are being sold on the market the clients will need roads to navigate them on. This leads to another expense of having to build miles of new roads. The cons definitely outweigh the pros of having driverless cars on the roads. Driverless cars are a dream that is waiting to happen in a future that we all hope to one day see, but they are not here yet. Driverless cars just aren't ready to be released into the world yet. Driverless cars still do require a driver at the wheel, they require a lot of new technology, and they are illegal in most states, even for testing purposes.

The first reason that driverless cars shouldn't be developed yet is because they aren't even fully driverless. Drivers would get bored waiting for their turn to drive. In order for drivers to not lose attention as they are driving, developers are hoping to bring in car entertainment and information systems with heads-up displays that can be turned off instantly when the driver needs to take over. However, the car can not turn off the display of a driver's phone which is more than likely the go-to option when bored. In this way, the in-car system is a big safetly concern as much as it is a safety feature.

The second reason that driverless cars shouldn't be in development yet is because of the amount of hardware and software that is required for a driverless car to function. Google's modified Toyota Prius uses position-estimationg sensors on the left rear wheel, a rotating sensor on the roof, a video camera mounted near the rearview mirror, four automotive radar sensors, a GPS receiver, and an inertial motion sensor. Can our current technology run all of these sensors and be able to process them quick enough for the car to make a decision on a road? Using driverless cars is not a good idea because cars are already dangerous as it is. To being using driverless cars as a form of transportation would be like trusting a machine with one's life. The pros of driverless cars are many, but the cons are just as plentiful. Driverless cars "would fundamentally change the world," however, they could just as easily ruin it (1).

Driverless cars are helpful because they do most of what true drivers hate to do. They drive. Such cars have the ability to "handle driving functions at speeds up to 25 mph" (7). The cars are also able to steer, accelerate, and stop. Driverless cars would "offer far more felxibility" and "use half the fuel of today's taxis" (1). Driverless cars can even drive several miles without any issues, but there is a lot that the cars cannot do on their own. The cars are not even completely driverless. A driver would jump for joy at the thought of a car that supposedly drives itself because that would mean relaxation for the driver, but is it truly all that relaxing?

Driverless cars can "steer, accelerate, and brake themselves" but they still require human skills. A driverless car would not actually mean no driving because the whole time a person is being driven, he or she must have his or her hands on the wheel. There are "special touch sensors" that "make sure the driver keeps hold of the wheel" (7). Driverless cars must not mean texting and driving becomes legal after all. Humans must stay alert while in driverless cars because accidents can still happen. The cars cannot navigate through construction sites or around accidents. Another issue with driverless cars is that they cannot pull in or out of driveways. Pulling out of a driveway or lot is typically the first action that a driver takes, and pulling in is typically the last action that a driver takes. If the trip has to start and end with the driver, what is the point of stopping just for the duration of the drive? "Why would anyone want a driverless car that still needs a driver" (8)?

Driving laws focus on keeping people in, or around, cars safe, but "safety is best achieved with alert drivers." The idea of driverless cars will automatically have drivers imagining everything that they could get done if they do not have to worry about operating the vehicle. There are sensors in driverless cars, but sensors will not stop people from doing what they want to do. Current driving laws do not even prevent people from doing what they want to do. If people cannot prevent accidents from happening, a machine will not be able to prevent accidents from happening.

Driverless cars can only be used once drivers learn how to operate cars. Cars are already not safe because of manufacturing errors and operator errors, so it is not smart to put the entire responsibility on a machine. When an accident occurs, "who is at fault--the driver or the manufacturer" (9)? The blame cannot be put on the car, but can it be put on the operator?

Driverless cars have been considered future technology and a distant dream for quite some time. While driverless cars have been around for a long time, as the article also states, they are currently a work in progress. I believe that driverless cars are the key to decreasing the number of accidents on the road; if there isn't a driver to be distracted, then there should be a lower chance of problems occuring on the road. Common causes of accidents on the road would be eliminated, such as drunk driving, texting while driving, and just simple absentmindedness. Due to the sensors and computer hardware and software, the car itself would be able to sense other cars and make driving safer. Since cars are machines, they wouldn't be subject to human folly either, and would solely be focused on driving its passengers to the designated location. GPS receivers also eliminate the problem with getting lost, and as such, I firmly believe that driverless cars will benefit humans and be a large step forward in public transportation. Driverless cars are, while still under development, able to drive as well as a human, and are equipped with the necessary electronics to sense obstacles and prevent accidents on the road.

The merits of driverless cars are not entirely limited to their sensors and programming. Inside of the car, with advanced technology, there's much more entertainment to be had. New inner displays offer up bigger screens and allow for the passenger to do something productive whilst not driving. This especially aids those who constantly get texts and calls, since they can now answer those texts and calls without fear of an accident. Additionally, the inner displays of the car can not only be used as entertainment, but to do productive work as well. Driving can be a quite tedious chore to do, especially during long car rides, and, moreoften than not, there are more productive things to be done. If the car drives itself, then the passenger inside is able to do much more than just sit and twiddle their thumbs, they can get ahead or finish up papers for work. This sort of technology gives people more time to whatever they so desire, and since time is so limited anyways, this can only be a good thing.

Although driverless cars take care of many of the problems that society has on the road today, I also think that there should be an override option in driverless cars. Perhaps in the future, when technology has advanced enough, there won't need to be an option for human interference, but as things are now, some situations call for cognitive ability. Driverless cars are automated programs, and as such, won't recognize spontaneous occurences, such as a child running out in front of the car. This is why I believe that back up functions should be implemented, such as the driver's seats which vibrate when the vehicle is in danger mentioned in the article, in order to keep everyone safe. Thus, I believe that the passengers have an obligation to, at the very least, be aware of their surroundings. However, it must also be noted that the merits outweigh the risks, and even the best technology is prone to an odd mishap.

In terms of public safety and technological advances, driverless cars are undeniably a step forward. Not only do they reduce the chance for roadside accidents, but they also allow the passengers inside to get more work done or relax. Despite being new technology, driveless cars already offer a plethora of new opportunities to people, and as such, can only keep society on an uphill climb in terms of technological advancements and wisdom.

To Drive or not to Drive

Many science fiction shows and novels create shining projections of the future. Common archetypes throughout these include futuristic architecture, appliances, and transportation. Although many children dreamed of these fantastic universes, some people believe that many of these seemingly impossible feats can be likely created in a time not too far from now. Companies such as Google, Tesla, Audi, and Nissan believe that driverless cars would be one of the first of the "future technologies" to roam the streets. These companies have taken the initiative in developing the driverless technologies, and are very optimistic about the results. However, as with all ideas, these driverless cars are full of flaws and safety concerns. However, despite the new issues that would arise, I believe that the development of these cars should definitely continue. This is because the driverless cars would have many benefits unseen in normal cars, and the flaws can be worked out over time.

The driverless cars offer much more versatility and freedom to the passenger, compared with the limits placed on passengers of a human driven car. The most obvious benefit is that the driverless cars would require little or no assistance from actual human drivers, allowing for more socializing between the passengers. Also, on instances such as long road trips, the driverless cars would allow the otherwise drivers to rest, rather than having to focus on the road for many hours straight. Also, according to the article, driverless cars could provide flexible public transport that would be more efficient in terms of fuel usage. Compared to the buses that have to stop multiple times along a route as well as taxis that require drivers, the driverless taxis would ferry along commuters quickly and in some cases would be more safe than trusting a stranger to drive you to a desired destination (taxi). The conveniences and flexibility that the driverless cars provide is a main reason why I am supportive of their development.

The article also brings up many negative points and flaws of these vehicles. Many of these flaws are convenience issues that are tied to safety. For example, the article states that Google's current drverless cars often require an actual driver to take over in situations such as pulling into and out of a driveway, or with traffic issues such as with roadwork or accidents. However, these issues are likely to be less of a concern as long as development continues, as new technology such as enhanced and more accurate sensors could allow for more precise navigation to avoid roadblocks or accidents. A possible solution for navigating driveways could be a customizable or programmable feature that allow owners of the car to program a sample route into the driveway that the car can then replicate using sensors to determine a set starting position. The article states that automakers also work on the assumption that the problems ahead will be solved, which is why I believe that as long as development is continued, improved technology and new ideas can solve many of the flaws of current driverless cars.

Some people wonder about the rules and regulations that would need to be put in place to ensure saftey as well as in the case that an accident does happen. For example, according to the article, people question who's fault it would be when an accident does happen, the owner of the car or the manufacturer? In the case that if the driver could have avoided the accident, then it is the fault of the driver. However, if it is a technological error that the driver has no control over, the liability would go to the manufacturer. Overall, the rules and regulations can adapt to the usage and development of the driverless cars, which is not a impossible conflict to solve.

Overall, the conveniences that a driverless car would provide far outweigh the problems that they create. Many of the flaws in current driverless cars can likely be fixed as technology improves, which is a process that would definitely occur as long as development continues. Even with normal cars, tehcnological flaws such as safety concerns are often recalled and fixed. Companies such as Toyota offer free fixes to safety concers they discover, proving that no car is without its flaws, driverless or not. Also, the development of autonmous cars could aslo assist in other fields of automation, and can demonstrate other purposes of the cars functions. I am completely for the continued development of autnomous cars because I believe they have the potential to become more efficient, convenient than normal cars. According to the article, Tesla, Mercedes-Benz, Audi, and Nissan have all projected a release of a mostly autonomous car by 2020. As shown by the engineers and scientists behind these driverless cars, the future is not as distant as it seems.

In the last couple of decades, car manufactures have made huge strides in automated features in cars. Newer cars are now being built with antilock brakes and exterior cameras that asist drivers in parking and warn them of objects in their path. Because of these technologies, many companies are trying to develop a driverless car that would be able to navigate the roads with minimal human engagement in the task. The idea sounds futuristic and innovative, but it is not without its problems. Driverless cars should not continue to be developed because they will reduce human readiness to take over in unpredictable situations, introduce issues of driver versus manufacturer liability, and require traffic laws to be re-written in every state.

The primary issue with driverless cars is one of safety. While it's true that driverless cars would reduce human error in speed and traffic violations, reliance on automation would cause drivers to be less prepared to take over when unpredictable situations arise. Without the constant practice and experience that drivers receive on the roads today, the driving skills of people with self-driving cars would rapidly decline. For instance, what if a child were to run out into the middle of the road? A normal driver would be able to react quickly because he or she would be focused on the task of driving and scanning his or her surroundings. A driver in an automated car however, would not have the same speedy response. Since he or she would be used to riding in the car as it drove itself and not actually driving, the situation might startle him or her more. The time it would take to switch from automated to manual driving would also be a factor. Automated cars, while decreasing some risk factors on the road, can't plan for every situation. Drivers need to be prepared and develop defensive driving skills through manual driving.

A second problem that comes up when considering whether to continue developing driverless cars is the issue of accountability in the case of an accident. If there was a mechanical issue in an automated car that caused an accident, it would be extremely difficult to tell whether the driver or the manufacturer was at fault. This dilemma would cause drivers to end up in countless court battles and responsible for legal expenses in a case that would be difficult to solve. Most people don't have the resources to go through such a lengthy and expensive process.

Finally, integrating driverless cars would necessitate a total reworking of traffic laws, state by state. Currently, traffic laws are only written for manually driven cars. It would take years to create acceptable laws and regulations in just one state. Getting legislation through in all fifty states would be an even slower process. The compromise would be to focus more time and energy on improving semi-automated car technology. By redirecting energy and resources here, drivers would still be in

control of the car, requiring fewer changes to current legislation, and more driving aides would be availible for drivers to use, increasing road safety.

Driverless cars may seem exciting and futuristic, but it's important to asses their practicality on the roads. Automated cars would reduce defensive driving skills and cause drivers to be less prepared to take over in unpredictable traffic situations. The integration of such cars would require existing traffic laws to be totally rewritten, and new legal problems would arise, such as the issue of driver versus manufacturer liability. It is far better to improve upon existing technologies and processes that we know work. The future may not resemble the sci-fi movies and television shows that everyone knows and loves, but it could be even better.

The development of driverless cars will revolutionize the future and is an important and positive goal that needs to be accomplished because driverless cars can reduce the number of fuel used, have sensors that can allow them to mimic the skill of a human driver, and provides a system that can keep the driver safe.

Reducing the amount of gasoline and other fossil fuels used in cars is one positive aspect that shows the necessity of driverless cars. Unlike regular cars that use fuel to move, these driverless cars use special tracks such as electrical cables and magnets with alternating polarity to drive. According to the author of the passage, "The track was embedded with an electrical cable that sent radio signals to a receiver on the front end of the car. Engineers at Berkeley tried something similar, but they used magnets with alternating polarity. The car read the positive and negative polarity as messages in binary code." This shows that not only are driverless cars more green and environment-friendly, but also shows that the driverless cars were so effecient that if it weren't for the expenses for upgrading for the existing roads, the smart-road systems could be implemented and practical.

The use of sensors that allow driverless cars to move in the same fashion as a human driver would is another positive factor that reveals the importance of building driverless cars. In driverless cars such as Google's modified Toyota Prius, these cars have different sensors that not only allow the car to conduct basic procedures such as moving forward, backward, and turning, but also have sensors that can scan the surrounding area in case of danger and obstructions. This can be shown in the passage where according to the author, "Google's modified Toyota Prius uses position-estimating sensors on the left rear wheel, a rotating sensor on the roof, a video camera mounted near the rearview mirror, four automative radar sensors, a GPS receiver, and inertial motion sensor. The most important bit of technology in this system is the spinning sensor on the roof. Dubbed LIDAR, it uses laser beams to form a constantly updating 3-D model of the car's surroundings. The combination of all this input is necessary for the driverless car to mimic the skill of a human at the wheel." This quote reveals that driverless cars have the technology to imitate the skills and instincts of a human driver, allowing tranportation to become much more flexible and convenient.

Having a system that can guarantee the safety of the driver is the final, positive trait that shows how much driverless cars can revolutionize the future. Although the driverless cars can conduct basic maneuvers such as accelerating, steering, and braking, the vehicles can always alert the driver to take over in case of complex situations such as navigating around work zones and accidents. According the passage, the author states, "They can steer, accelerate, and brake themselves, but all are designed to notify the driver when the road ahead requires human skills, such as navigating through work zones and around accidents. This means the human driver must remain alert and be ready to take over when the situation requires. This necessitates the car being ready to quickly get the driver's attention whenever a problem occurs." This quotation reveals that a driver's safety is guaranteed when both the car and the driver work together when getting to a destination. While the car can safely and easily drive the driver to his or her destination under normal condition, the driver can take over in case of unexpected and complicated situations, guaranteeing that both the driver and the car can remain safe.

Despite many states opposing the idea and development of driverless cars due to certain negative aspects, the construction, researching, and testing of these vehicles reveal postive factors that overwhelm the negative ones. Many have envisioned a future where a future where the public transportation system is dominated by driverless cars that offer far more flexibility than a bus or taxi, and despite the long road needed to be taken in order to achieve this goal, it is a road worth taking. The development will be able to change the future forever and is something needed to be accomplished due to the ability to reduce the amount of gasoline and other fossil fuels, provide sensors that can travel in a human-like manner, and establish a cooperation system that can guarantee the safety of the driver and the car.

Driverless cars are an incredible technological innovation that, at a time, we only only thought we'd see in movies and on television. Aside from being an interesting concept for Hollywood use, driverless cars would also have a very large impact on society. Roads would become safer, with a computer making carefully calculated decisions for the best of the passenger and other drivers, but the job market would also shift greatly. Alternatively, the roads could also become a more dangerous place, due to the possible failure of computer-controlled cars. Such an innovation would likely be a double-edged sword in terms of the impact it would have.

In terms of having a positive influence on traffic safety, driverless cars excel. A driverless car can carefully map out the entire environment around it in an instant, and make decisions accordingly. This eliminates the possibility for mistakes on the driver's part. This also brings about the possibility of getting around in a vehicle without the aid of others for people with disablities, such as people who are blind or have impairments that prevent them from being able to drive. However, the driver doesn't have to give up complete control of the vehicle, being able to take over whenever necessary. All in all, it becomes a luxury of convenience for drivers and a safety measure as well.

Unfortunately, this idea isn't without faults. It's unlikely that these vehicles would see consumer use, due to the amount of upkeep they would require, the attentiveness required of a driver to take over at a moment's notice, and situations in which the car may not know what to do. While these cars notify drivers when to take over, there are many situations in which the driver may not be able to respond to such a notification, such as the driver sleeping or playing very loud music. This could result in an accident and the endangerment of lives.

With the creation of such vehicles also brings a change in the job market. With further development and entirely computer-controlled taxis, the need for drivers disappears almost completely. This would cause an economic catastrophe for such businesses.

The idea of a driverless car being able to know where to go implies that it will implement the use of GPS. What, then, does the car do in the event that it loses signal? The vehicle may be able to download the entire map of the GPS route before departure, or it may leave the driver up to their own devices. If a driver is asleep or unattentive when the car loses signal, there is a question of whether or not it will keep driving and predict where to go, or if it will pull over until the driver is able to take over.

The final issue with this concept is the event that someone else is harmed or endangered. If the car causes an accident and injures or kills a pedestrian, is it the fault of the car manufacturer or the owner of the car? There is no way to really justify either side of the argument. Furthermore, the car's job seems to be to protect the driver over anything else. In a hypothetical situation, such as if the driver is in danger, but swerving, braking quickly, or any other maneuver to protect a single driver is guaranteed to put the lives of ten people outside of the vehicle at risk, does that car make that decision? A person would put their own life at risk to avoid taking the lives of others in this situation, but would the car do the same, or would it run several people over to protect itself and the driver? The idea of morality in a vehicle is unconventional to consider, but it does bring up important questions.

Overall, while the concept and implementation of driverless cars is an amazing innovation and has many uses and applications, it also causes many problems that do not yet have answers. Perhaps, with time, these problems will be adressed and solved. Until then, taking drivers out of vehicles is not in the best interest of the public. In an age where everything is becoming automated over time, vehicles still have a long way to go.

The future is an exciting and wonderous concept. Many people believe the future will hold all sorts of technological advances. One of these much awaited advances is that of the driverless car. People believe this car will make their life easier and far more fun. However, the idea of the driverless car has many faults which could potentially cause serious injury or great conflict. Despite the appealing nature of it, the driverless car should not be developed further.

When driving, the number one concern of the driver is the safety of their person and every other person in the car with them. Driverless cars provide a great threat to all of these people. The possibility of a one hundred percent driverless vehicle is less than likely. Despite all the advances made, the car will still need a driver ready to assist or take over when needed. The success of the switch between driverless car to a driver depends entirely on the reaction rate of the driver. If the driver happened to fall asleep on a long car trip and the car needed a driver to take over, then the car would most likely end up crashing. Companies in the business of creating driverless cars want the cars to include "in-car entertainment and information systems that use heads-up displays" (8). Companies claim these displays would immediately turn off when the driver needed to take over and therefore be classified as a safety feature. However, these displays would hinder the driver and endanger everyone in the car. By distracting the driver and causing them to relax, these displays keep the driver from being prepared to immediately ake control of the car, which can result in a car crash fatal to all of the car's occupants.

In addition to hindering the safety of those in the car, the driverless car endangers those around and outside the car. The safety on the roads depends entirely on how well the driver is following the law. Driverless cars would have to be able to read, comprehend, and act upon every road sign along the road as well as be aware of the lines on the actual road and other cars. Several common actions drivers take while driving, such as passing, depend not on signs, but on the driver's proximity to other drivers. The result of any of these actions being taken at a wrong time can result in a large and fatal collision. The lack of preparedness from the driver that the car causes can also be detrimental to other drivers on the road. If a driver is not prepared to take over, they could end up doing a number of dangerous actions that could cause a multiple car crash or could potentially harm pedestrians, depending on the road the car is on.

All of the information about the driverless car has a disturbing lack of safety precautions. All of the precautions mentioned are for when the car is driving. They say nothing about how to be safe before the car begins to drive. For example, what is to prevent children from entering the car and accidentaly or purposely driving off. If this occurs, the child would be in terrible danger if the car needed a driver to take over. If the hopes of the businesses creating these cars is accurate, all the child would need to do to activate and drive the car is to insert the key and place their hand on the wheel. However, this does not only apply to children. This principle can apply to any person without a liscence as well. Even if their driver's liscence had been revoked, they would still be able to operate the driverless car. In addition, what extra precautions would be taken to prevent the car from driving off without a driver. If the equipment were to fault while the car was in a carrage or in a parking lot, the car could cause great injury, massive amounts of property damage, and potentially the deaths of those nearby.

Like all new inventions, lawsuits are a major concern for many of the parties involved. In order to have driverless cars, laws would have to be put into place to protect both the driver and the manufacturer. The main question that would be asked is "if the technology fails and someone is injured, who is at fault-the driver or the manufacturer" (9)? This question will cause numerous court cases and conflicts as both sides try to defend themselves and prevent the blame from falling upon them. At every wreck or malfunction of the vehicle, there would be those feverently trying to win a lawsuit.

Driverless cars appear to be something out of our wildest hopes and dreams about the future and, while flawless in vision, the reality is far from perfect. These new driverless cars could cause a number of issues including, but not limited to, the compromised safety of those inside the car, the compromised safety of those around and outside the car, and numerous lawsuits. Despite seeming to be an amazing new invention, the driverless car should remain what it always has been, wishful thinking.

Driverless cars are not a good or safe choice for drivers. There are many negative aspects of the idea of these types of cars. They are more expensive, less enjoyable for drivers, can't self operate in all conditions and the driver is unaware of when they will need to take over. Also, they are not rendered completely safe and new laws would need to be passed for people to be able to operate them. In the event of an accident, the idea of who would have to claim responsibility is uncertain. The probability of an accident happening due to technology glitching would be quite high. These cars would be a bad idea because they pose a big threat.

To begin, driverless cars would be more expensive for everyone. The manufacturers would have to splurge and spend much more money on specific parts for the driverless cars. Engineers at Berkely designed a car that read positive and negative polarity as messages in binary code, which required a smart road system that worked very well, "but they required upgrades to existing roads, something that was simply too expensive to be practical." (paragraph 3) This tells us that the engineers had a good idea, but lots of roads would've needed renovations that were far too expensive. Next, driverless cars would be less enjoyable for drivers. "Why would anyone want a driverless car that still needs a driver? Wouldn't drivers get bored waiting for their turn to drive?" (paragraph 8) It wouldn't be fun sitting and doing nothing in the driver's seat when you aren't the one driving. Drivers would need to be alert at all times due to another negative aspect mentioned earlier: the driver is unaware as to when they will need to take over. "...the human driver must remain alert and be ready to take over when the situation requires. This necessitates the car being ready to quickly get the driver's attention whenever a problem occurs." (paragraph 7) The drivers must keep their eyes on road and devote their 100% attention to driving even while the car is doing the braking, steering and accelerations itself. Driverless cars also cannot drive in all conditions. "...all are designed to notify the driver when the road ahead requires human skills, such as navigation through work zones and around accidents." (paragraph 7) Drivers are never really free of driving, so purchasing a car that is said to be driverless for the purpose of not having to drive is pointless. Drivers have to drive themselves through things like constuction or accident sites.

Furthermore, driverless vehicles are not legally rendered completely safe. "...traffic laws are written with the assumption that the only safe car has a human driver in control at all times." (paragraph 9) This proves that driverless cars legally cannot be considered safe because the human behind the wheel is not in control at all times. The car itself would be in control presumably for the majority of the time alloted for driving, so by law it isn't considered safe. With that being said, new laws would need to be passed in order for the driverless cars to be tested/driven. "Still even if traffic laws change, new laws will be needed in order to cover liability in the case of an accident." (paragraph 9) This directly tells us that new laws wouild need to be passed before people could legally own and operate driverless vehicles. This leads into the next idea: the responsibility of an accident involving a driverless car would be hard for one to claim. "If the technology fails and someone is injured, who is at fault-the driver or the manufacturer?" (paragraph 9) Since the driver is supposed to remain alert and be ready to jump in when the car can't handle a certain situation, who should take the blame for an accident? The car for the technology failing or the human for not taking over before the accident occured?

In conclusion, driverless vehicles would not be a good idea. Testing them in controlled environments where humans being put into danger isn't a factor would be okay, but for recreational use only. These cars would be more expensive, can't drive in all conditions, are less fun for drivers, and not rendered completely safe. The drivers wouldn't know when they would need to take over until right when they're needed to, new laws would need to be passed for them and the responsibility of an accident would be uncertain. Overall, these driverless cars are just a bad idea and pose a big threat to humans because the probability of an accident happening would be more likely, especially since the technology could glitch easier and faster than a human could mess up on the road and cause an accident.

The largest problem with driverless cars is the legalities that go along with them. Various advancements in the practicality of driverless vehicles have been made in the past few years. Companies like Google and BMW devote hundreds of hours to coming up with new solutions/technologies to further along the advancement of independent cars. There is one issue with the concept of autonomous cars, however: they aren't practical in the first place.

Vehicles (which aren't even in the market yet) that are so called "driverless" still require a driver. Companies have developed warning signals to notify the driver when their assistance is needed. The text states, "GM has developed seats that vibrate when the vehicle is in danger of backing into an object." Google also has their own version of a warning system: "The Google car simply announces when the driver should be prepared to take over." Why would a consumer buy a "driverless" car when they still have to remain alert? Another company, BMW, requires that the driver of a "driverless" car must keep their hands on the wheel at all times: "The car can handle driving functions up to 25 mph, but special touch sensors make sure the driver keeps hold of the wheel." These independent vehicles are still co-dependent on an alert driver.

The actual consumer usage of a driverless car isn't the only practical issue. According to the text, "Presently, traffic laws are written with the assumption that the only safe car has a human driver in control at all times. As a result, in most states it is illegal even to test computer-driven cars." Traffic laws would have to be completely rewritten in order for driverless vehicles to be allowed on roads.

Even if autonomous vehicles are some day introduced to the market, old-fashioned cars, complete with a driver, will still be at large. The article brings up the issue of vehicular accidents: "If the technology fails and someone is injured, who is at fault---the driver or the manufacturer?" If a driverless car crashes into a car with a driver, whose fault is it? A manufacturing company promises that their product is driverless. The consumer buys the product, under the assumption that he/she can sit back, relax, and let the car do their work. Shortly after, there's a sixty car pile-up on Highway 50. Would the consumer be allowed to sue the manufacturer for false advertising? Would the manufacturing company be allowed to retort that the consumer didn't pay attention to whatever warning signals they had built into the vehicle? The whole issue is messy and definitely not practical.

Driverless vehicles are a nice idea. People like whatever makes things easier for them. However, independent cars are unfortunately just not practical. For the most part, driverless vehicles aren't really driverless. They require the consumer to remain aware of their surroundings. Traffic laws would need to be completely rethought. Court issues involving vehicular accidents turn into a blurry, grey mess. Companies will continue to work on the advancement of autonomous cars, but ultimately their efforts will be in vain.

Driverless cars are one more step to an accident-free driving world. Like any technology, it will take years to refine and will generate controversy along the way. However, these potential setbacks should not distract from the ultimate goals of new car technologies such as autonomy; to improve and refine the driving experience. Driverless snd autonomus cars will be a huge step forward in car technology, helping to improve road safety, efficiency, and comfort.

Driverless cars will improve the safety of people traveling in them and around them. As is stated in the article, partially autonomous vehicles are already on the roads today, from the likes of Mercedes, BMW, Tesla, and others. While these cars cannot in any way drive without a driver, certain features allow them to cruise on "autopilot" at certain speeds in certain conditions. Mercedes, BMW, and Teslas' flagship sedans all have this feature embedded into their adaptive cruise control settings, meaning the car will manage the throttle, brakes, and steering to maintain one's lane, speed, and will keep an appropriate distance to the cars around it. All of this means the potential for human misjudgement to cause a crash is greatly reduced, and as more cars get these features, getting ever closer to full autonomy, the roads will only become safer.

Driverless and autonomous cars will not only aid in making driving safer, they will contribute to making cars more efficient and eco-friendly. This claim can be backed-up by simply examining the technologies currently seen in cars and their effects on efficiency. The automatic gearbox, smart engine technologies such as cynlinder deactivation, fuel-saving measures taken by vehicles to improve efficiency in any way, all of these work in similar ways as driverless cars will; sensors, computers, and machinery all work together to sense the world around the car and adjust for the best efficiency possible. With driverless cars, the throttle, braking, steering, speed, light-brightness, gear, engine condition, and wheel condition can all be changed by conputers in order to make the car more efficient. Already, semi-autonomous cars like the Mercedes and Teslas' discussed earlier employ some of these technologies in their "autopilot" modes to improve their efficiency. This demonstrates how cars of the future will use driverless technologies to drastically improve their efficiency.

Last, but certainly not least, driverless cars will be more comfortable than modern cars. If the experience of driving is broken down to its most basic form, it is a chore. Of course, there will always be those who love driving as a sport or hobby, but the majority of people will no doubt love to be driven rather to drive. Driverless cars can make this a reality in just a couple decades. Many car compaines have already begun investing in a future in which a car becomes more like first class seating on an airplane, with seats that swivel around and recline to make the time spent in a car a relaxing break from the hectic world. These cars will have a completely different cabin architecture than the cars on the roads today. There will be no need for a steering wheel, for driver controls or even a drivers seat. This makes seeing concepts of these future cars put out by GM or Mercedes like looking at an alien spacecraft, but the technologies to achieve those designs are just a few years away.

Driverless cars will improve just about every aspect of driving for the majority of people. The roads will become safer, the cars will burn through less fuel and achieve more with it, and the experience will become more confortable than ever before. And all of this, this seemingly futuristic dream technology, is just around the corner. The rate at which this technology is growing is very exciting. In just a couple years, many of the cars made by some of the worlds most prestigious car companies will feature some degree of autonomous driving, the first step toward full autonomy. The future of driving is reaching a new era, but the question is, are we willing to leave this part of our lives to our technology?

As a result, many states in the United States have "limited [the] use of semi-autonomous cars".

If even the activity of semi-autonomous is limited, surely the laws concerning fully autonomous will be much more strict.

Technology is known to fail in certain situations and is not completely reliable.

In the case that a driverless car were to be involed in a accident, the liabilty of the case would not be clear, and it would be hard to determine whether "the driver or the manufacturer" is at fault.

Overall the introduction of driverless cars would not be beneficial, if compared to current cars, due to the fact that it would have to result in the development of new laws, and the issue of liabilty would not be clear.

In order for a driverless car to work, it must have the capability to analyse its surroudings as a human would.

Although sensors are extraordinary inventions to aid electronic devices to understand the world,

The inefficiency of using sensors on a driverless car supports the notion that such cars should not be produced.

It is true that Google has created cars that "have driven more than hald a million miles without a crash", but "Google cars aren't truly driverless".

Being in a fully driverless car poses a great risk to the passenger, because there is always the possibility that "the technology fails and someone [will be] injured".

For that reason, it is not a good idea for fully autonomous cars to be developed.

There are many issues that are inhibiting the introduction of driverless cars

into society such as problems with liabilty, the unreliability of current technology, and the issues of safety that are involved.

There is still much research that has yet to be done before determining if the innovation of a driverless car would be plausible for everyday life.

Although currently, the idea of a fully driverless car does not seem acceptable by many people, there may come a day when it will become normal for someone to own such a car.

If the level of technology continues to improve, and the changes of traffic regulations and liability laws are done, then the introduction of an autonomous car will be more than likely to occur in the future.

Yes, driverless cars may benefit the economy in some ways but the risks outweight the benefits. Driverless cars are not only hazardous to the pedestrians but also the person sitting behind the steering wheel.

In the article, it's stated that some manufacturing companies are coming up with ideas to install video monitors to allow the person behind the steering wheel to watch when waiting for their turn to drive. Personally, I would not feel safe riding in a car that does all of the work for me. The vehicle could malfunction putting pedestrians and myself in danger. Yes, avoiding hazardous situations may not be a choice at most times but the ability to park and brake when needed are a choice. People of the world may become lazy and believe that switching to a driverless car is the greatest option when really, their choice is being over ridden by their laziness.

I hope that not only myself but others can see the risks and dangers when using or allowing driverless cars on the roadways. Using a computer driven car to take photos of the world is one thing but allowing robots to overtake our roads is another. I strongly urge that driverless cars be forgotten about. Our economy and lives do not need to be endulged in any more threatening situations than they already are. Driverless cars are not the future of this world.

Should people really trust all these fancy sensors, and technology to transport themselves and others safely? Driverless cars have been a goal of auto manufacturers for years.

But are they really a plausible idea?

Can they really be considered an upgrade from human drivers?

Would thier creation have more positives than negatives?

I, personally, do not believe so.

Driverless cars are simply too hard to implement into today's driving system and, generally, the benefits of these cars pale in comparison to their negatives.

First of all, driverless cars would require massive changes to driving laws.

For example, if there were a wreck between a driverless cars due to technology failure and people were injured, who is at fault?

Even with specific laws covering this topic, it would be incredibly difficult to create laws that would fairly cover the issue in its entirety.

Would passengers be considered at fault for failure to react in time?

Or would manufacturers be held responsible for their failure to produce a perfectly functional vehicle?

How could consumers be protected from situations like this?

How would manufacturers respond to such situations?

Given that most driving laws are designed to be safe and protect all individuals involved, can implementing something with so many uncertainties really be a good idea?

Another issue with driverless is cars is exactly how driverless they are.

While the end goal is to produce a car that requires no human skills to manuver, what happens in the mean time?

The "driverless" cars currently being produces all require some sort of human interaction.

Should a problem occur, a human driver would have to take control right?

Google's car, for example, will alert the driver of when they should be prepared to take over in the case of an accident or road construction.

Meaning that in the end, humans will still have to drive the car.

If a human driver is still required for these "driverless" cars to function, then why purchase one considering they would likely be higher in price than regular cars?

Other than a slight convienience, what benefits do these "driverless" cars really impose?

Lastly, how would these cars react to other human drivers?

Let's say these cars are created in the near future.

Naturally, some people will not want a driverless car due to personal preference.

So you have these driverless cars on the road with other human drivers who are incredibly unpredictable.

How many accidents happen because a person tries to get over when they do not have enough room or due to human confusion?

Even with today's advanced sensory technology, how would these cars handle these specific situations?

Hand to control to the human driver?

By the time the human takes the wheel or becomes aware of the situation, will it not be too late?

Should someone run a red light and the car is about to be side-swiped, what will happen?

Driverless cars are the item of the future that many auto manufacturers hope to finalize soon.

Are they a plausible idea in my opinion?

No.

Can they be considered an upgrade from human drivers in my opinion?

No, not neccessarily.

Would their creation have more positives than negatives?

No, I do not believe so.

Driverless cars are an interesting topic and would be an amazing technological feat, but without a drastic change in today's world and society, they are just too hard to implement into our everyday lives.

"So what lies ahead for the autonomous car?"

This question is given on the topic of driverless cars in the article, "Driverless Cars are Coming".

The world has begun a new age of development in transportation, and there are many people looking to find new, self-driving vehicles to become a part of our society.

The author of this story presents both postive and negative aspects on the idea of a driverless car, and there are multiple advocates for each side of the argument.

With examples and points made by this article, anyone can propose an argument for or against this new idea.

When it comes to vehicles, it doesn't seem particularly good to have those without someone to monitor what is happening.

In real life situations, people should be in control of cars, or at least be monitoring how they are moving.

One quote states, "In fact, none of the cars developed so far are comepletely driverless." This quote shows us that out of many of the driverless cars that have been made already, there are still limitations to what they can do. Even though driverless cars are capable of many things, humans still have to be there in cases of emergency.

This is further shown in the statement, "They can steer, accelerate and brake themselves, but all are designed to notify the driver when the road ahead requires human skills, such as navitgating through work zones and around accidents."

As of now, cars are not yet comepletely self-driving because there are certain things that only a person can do to keep all passengers safe.

With more improvements, driverless vehicles could be something postive for people everywhere, but until there are more advancements, we cannot be sure that these self-driving vehicles are in the best interest of everyone.

A major roadblock for driverless cars is safety.

If there is no driver at the wheel of a car, then how can someone be sure they will not get into an accident?

In the article is it stated, "Lawmakers know that safety is best achieved with alert drivers." This shows that cars can be unsafe if a driver is not aware of what is happening, or if there is not driver at

all.

A person who can see and react to what is infront of them is important, especially on the roads.

In addition to that, another quote says, "This means a human must remain alert and be ready to take over when the situation requires." As stated previously, cars are not yet able to be fully driverless.

There must be someone to ensure safety of the passengers in case an obstacle presents itself.

If there is constuction or an accident with self-driving vehicles that are available now, a human must take control to manuver in the situation. Therefore, driveless cars should remain off the road until manufacturers are positive that the vehicles will be able to keep everyone is as safe as possible in any possible situation.

In conclusion, driverless cars don't seem like safe ways of moving forward with innovation and technology right now.

The article, "Driverless Cars are Coming," gives both evidence for and against the possibiltiies to a self-driving car.

While having many pros, there are still a number cons to go with them.

So, even though there are many good things that can come out of not having to drive yourself places all of the time, there are still many issues with a machine being able to complete a human task.

Technology is making huge advancements, but until we are able to ensure that driverless cars can both effectively and safely transport people, they should remain as a idea for the future.

that is able to drive fully automated at speeds up to 25 miles per hour, but only if the driver keeps both hands on the steering wheel. This invention of BMW's not only brings a safe form of automation to modern cars, but also brings a relaxing break to driver's who need it.

Most people would be like "yes, this is a great idea!" but they don't take in consideration the dangers of this "driverless" car. The car can only do so much but certain human skills are needed while driving. Therefore, the safest way to drive a car is with a human in control at all times.

Most people would question themselves how the car really works. Well the answer is, sensors. According to "Driverless Cars Are Coming", the driverlesss car has sensors on the left rear wheel, a roating sensor on the roof, a video camera mounted near the rearview mirrow, four automotive radar sensors, a GPS receiver, and an internal motion sensor. It also has an antilock sensor so the car will be able to know when to break and what not. The driverless car can reach up to 25 mph at the most. These qualities can drive a car but is it really considered a "safe" car?

What do you do when you reach a point where there are accidents and work zone areas? Of course the car is technologically smart enough to drive itself, but there are certain situations that require human skills to be able to navigate the car. According to the BMW company, the driverless car has "alerts" that notifies the driver when to take over. For example, the driver's seat vibrates to notify the driver when the vehicle is backing into an object and flashing lights on the windshield notify a heads-up display. These alerts are somewhat helpful to the driver to let them know when to take over but is it still safe to drive it, be a passenger in the car, or be one of the surrounding cars or pedestrians around the car?

If the car was really safe wouldn't it be popular now and used everywhere around the world? The traffic law says that the only safe car has a human driver in control and alert of its surroundings at all times. In most states it's illegal to even test computer-driven cars. Imagine you are in a rush to work and are already 10 minutes late. The Driverless Car can only go up to 25 mph. That's not even the speed limit for most streets. Only a human would be able to drive faster and in full control. Let's hypothetically say that one of those driverless cars were to get in an accident. Who's fault would it be? The driver or the manufacturer of the car? Most people would argue that it's the driver's fault for not being cautious but isn't that what the whole point of the car is for? To be able to drive in any circumstances. The driver can't control the car itself, the driver is only there when needed. The safest way to drive a car is with a human in control at all times. Only a human has the skills of knowing its every surrounding and will be cautious enough to know what to do in certain situations.

A driverless car may sound cool and all but it's not the safest way to get around town. There are certain situations that require human skills like knowing how to drive on the interstate, driving around work zone areas, or through accidents. Even busy streets are a big thing! The best way to maintain everyone safe is to have a driver in control of the vehicle at all times. I mean, would you still want to get in a driverless car after knowing what the consequences could be?

I don't exactly know whether I agree or disagree with driverless cars. Their are plenty of advantages to driverless cars. But we all know the first thing people think about when they hear "driverless car" is how cool and it would be to not have to control your car while driving. But not too many think about the disadvantages we would run into. The past has shown us plenty of times what can happen when we depend on technology too much. It's easy to survive dropping you phone in the middle of the mall, but imagine your car malfunctioning on the middle of the highway late at night.

One disadvantage of a driverless car to me is people becoming too dependant. In Indiana you can legally obtain a license at the age of 16, so in the future we could possibly have all driverless cars, which means you can have a license and not know how to drive an actual car. What if one day companies come out and say all their cars have to shut down for a week and all we have are regular cars? No one will know what to do because they're so used to letting their car do the driving. Say you have to be to a very important meeting and you're depending on your car to get you there on time and you get into a car crash 2 years after you've had your driverless car. Do you have the right to be angry at or even sue the car company? Because you arent't doing the driving, the car is. There's so much you wont have control over in a driverless car, so if anything goes wrong, what do you do?

Another thing is getting too comfortable using a driverless car. We all know a friend or family member who isn't trusted to drive because they get sleepy at the wheel, imagine if there is no wheel. What do you do if something goes wrong? Maybe you've had your driverless car for some years so you're used to it functioing pretty well, so now you're riding and on your phone or looking in the back seat and talking to your friends that are with you. If anything sudden happens to where the car cant react fast enough and you have no control what will you do? Say theres a semi infront of you and it suddenly stops, and the car does pick it up in time and stops too, but the car behind you isn't driverless and the driver cant react in time, then they crassh you from behind. With a regular car you could've gotten out of the way instead of just stopping forcing the car behind you to either stop immediately or crash you.

But there are also some advantages one is being able to multi-task. Adults have mornings where they wake up late and have to get ready then drive to work. With a driverless car, you could (if needed) finish your hair and/or makeup while on your way to your destination. If you haven't had time to eat, instead of trying to balance your coffee and eating a bagel, you could take your time and eat and even prepare your food while driving. Or maybe you aren't good at having your focus on different things at once but you're a busy person. You could talk on the phone and not have to worry about being too focused on the road.

Another one is the car assiting your driving. Maybe the car could react to an on-coming accident before you could. Maybe you take the same route to work everyday, the car could help show you newer or faster ways to get there. What if one day you're in a rush and you're driving then run into a construction site. The car's GPS could've helped detect that and avoided it and got you where you needed to be faster.

In conclusion, to me there are a lot of things you can be helped with by a driverless car. But, at the same time you have to consider the disadvantages and the downsides to it all. Like I said before, history has shown what could happen if we depend on technology too much. So to me driverless cars could go either good or bad.

Imagine if you are driving down the street one day and are suddenly hit by a car; however, when you get out to talk to the driver you find that there is not one. Today, this would be shocking to most people, but in the near future it may become a reality. The world has always been fascinated with the prospect of driverless cars and the potential benefits of them, but the consequences far outweigh those benefits. Driverless cars could cause arguements between the manufacturer and the consumer, are not always completely driverless, and will cause a negative impact on society rather than a positive one.

The goal of a driverless car is stated in its name-- driverless. The cars that have been developed so far, however, still need a driver behind the wheel in certain situations, such as work zones and accident sites (paragraph 7). Various companies have created ways to notify the driver of when they must take control of their vehicle, but then the vehicle is no longer driverless. When the technology is developed so that the car is completely driverless, there is the possibilty for gliltches in the system, which could cause an accident. This leads to the issue of liability. As stated in paragraph 9, "who is at fault--the driver or the manufacturer?" New laws will have to be created and arguements between the manufacturer and the consumer may result. Regardless of these consequences, some people still see driverless cars as a positive.

Many believe that driverless cars will have a positive impact on our society and are advocating for their development. As stated in paragraph 5, they believe that "information from the sensors can cause the car to apply brakes on individual wheels and reduce power from the engine, allowing far better response and control than a human driver could manage alone." Some people feel that driverless cars are safer, especially in regards to bad drivers. Another benefit of driverless cars is the potential for "in-car entertainment and information systems that use heads-up displays" as a substitute for people attempting to illegally text and drive (paragraph 8). Many people feel that driverless cars are safer but have not considered the consequences of them.

Although some people believe that driverless cars would be safer, driverless cars would be just as dangerous as a normal driver if not more so. They have the potential to malfunction at any time. Driverless vehicles present another problem as well-- the possibility of drivers becoming bored waiting for their turn to drive. As stated in paragraph 8, "The psychological aspects of automation are really a challenge." This is yet another problem for manufacturers to try to solve and a negative benefit of driverless cars.

In recent years, the reality of driverless cars has become more and more real. Society needs to ask itself "is this really a good thing?". The potential benefits of driverless cars are few and far between compared to the consequences. Disputes between the consumer and manufacturer, drivers becoming bored, and driverless cars that are not really driverless are just a few of the negative aspects of continuing to develop driverless cars.

A married mother hops into her new driverless car and begins her route to the grocery store. As she casually browses her phone, the car approaches a roundabout. The sensors on the car's sides do not notice the slight curve of the road, and the car fails to slow down or wait for its turn. The mother, not paying attention, is alerted to return to the wheel. However, it is too late; the car slams into a motorcycle driven by a young, newlywed man, killing both the man and the mother with the impact. Such a scenario is extremely likely to occur in the near future. Google is currently developing a car that can function without a driver at the wheel at all times. These driverless cars are said to be the future of transportation in urban areas, for they are thought to be more efficient and faster than current automobiles. This excerpt from the text implies that companies want to make transportation an entertaining, recreational experience. This, however, is a very harmful way of thinking. If people decide driving is not a serious issue, crashes and accidents will occur much more frequently. Sometimes, a situation calls for human intellect to determine the best thing to do. If a car has a mind of its own, how will one know what to expect from his or her own car as well as the cars around it?

Many individuals will argue that driverless cars are extremely beneficial and will be the 'car of the future'. Some may claim that driverless cars will allow all people to have the opportunity for solitary transportation, unlike buses or taxis. People with physical disabilities might be able to drive a car on their own. Supporters of driverless cars may argue that these vehicles are faster and more efficient with money. Others will state that the use of gas will decrease if driverless cars are put into effect. Although all of these ideas are possible, they are not necessarily true.

Human-driven cars are currently being modified and will potentially exceed the benefits presented with driverless cars. Many companies are creating battery-powered cars that will eliminate the need for gas altogether. These vehicles will be much more economically efficient and safer for the environment than any gas-powered car, whether it is human-driven or driverless. Human-driven vehicles in Japan have also been made that can be driven by those with physical disabilities. Driverless cars are not fit for society because there are too many situations that can not rely on technology alone. Countless accidents have been prevented because the driver was quick and smart enough to avoid the crash. Suppose a driver must avoid a crash by veering off the road. A driverless car might decide to crash into a concrete building instead of a stack of hay bales on the other side of the road, simply because it lacked human intellect. Paragraph 7 states, "This necessitates the car being ready to quickly get the driver's attention whenever a problem occurs." This means that if the car fails to get the driver's attention, the car will crash; this leaves the most important question- was it the driver's fault or the manufacturer's fault? The only way to avoid this situation is by avoiding the use of driverless cars.

Clearly, driverless cars are not as incredible as they seem. Creating a car with no need for a driver will result in the laziness of society, a rise in accidents, and complicated conflicts with the law. Human-driven cars are a much safer way of transportation and will be more beneficial to society in the long run. Opposers of driverless cars should raise awareness of the many dangers of driverless vehicles and should help others recognize the countless benefits of human-driven vehicles.

Have you ever wondered what it would be like if the world had cars that drove on their own? This would be a bad thing, and could potentially cause more accidents. The three main reasons this is a bad idea are; the cost is extrememly high, people may not pay attention, and the cars can't completely drive on their own.

The first problem with smart cars, is that the cost for the equipment and technology is too expensive. According to the article, the track for General Motor's concept car required massive upgrades to the roads that exist today, and the price was just too expensive to be practical. Google's modified Toyota Prius has, and uses, a rotating sensor on the roof, position-estimating sensors on the left rear wheel, a GPS receiver, a video camera mounted near the rearview mirror, an internal motion sensor, and four automotive radar sensors. Just imagine the money it would take to put all of that into each car that is made by google. The people just simply can afford it. Just the spinning sensor on the roof uses laser beams to form a constantly updating 3-D model of the car's surroundings. It is the most important thing on the car, and probably the most expensive.

The next problem with these experimental cars would be that the human inside the car may not be paying attention. The cars are designed with entertainment and information systems on the inside of the car, for the driver to use while waiting for their turn to drive. They do have a button to turn them off instantly when the driver needs to take over, but what if the driver continues to use them while drving.These may very well distract the driver, and could lead to an accident. The car has warnings , but what if the driver thinks that the car can handle driving on its own, even with the warnings? The driver may think that he or she is safe because they are in a smart, driverless car. Even with all of the enertainment systems, the driver will have nothing to keep them alert and awake in the long stretches of time that the car will be driving on its own. The driver may very well fall asleep.

The last and final problem with these smart cars are the fact that they are not completely driverless. The driver still needs to be at the wheel when the car is in motion. The cars can not control themselves at speeds over 25mph. This means that on most roads, the car would not be able to drive itself. The cars cannot back out of driveways or work their way through work zones, and accidents, so the driver would still have to be ready to take the wheel in times of need.

In conclusion, the idea of a smart, driverless car is very dangerous. The production of thses cars may lead to over expensive and too high prices, distractions/ falling asleep while in the car, and possible accidents because the car cannot drive through certain obtructions on its own. The cars could be very dangerous to society, and may cause many more accidents than are currently happening in today's world.

Driverless cars are an idea that many advanced technology specialist hope for. When the word, "driverless," is passed around, society doesn't logically ponder the idea, but rather enjoys the thought of possibly sleeping while your car drives for you. The real issue is the danger in the possibilities of the car malfunctioning while the driver is asleep, because they trusted their car. In the article, "Driverless Cars Are Coming," the idea of one day having cars that drive for us is introduced, which is definitely an awful idea.

Trusting one's car to drive itself safely and deliver the human behind the wheel safely to their destination is rediculous. The author explains, "They can steer, accelerate, and brake themselves, but all are designed to notify the driver when the road ahead requires human skills, such as navigating through work zones and around accidents." Manufacturers of these semi-autonomous vehicles believe when the car requires assistance from a human, it will alert the driver. However, not all humans immediately awake to vibrations and sounds. Therefore, if the vehicle fails to alert the driver to retain control and resolve the issue, an accident or further issues will definitely occur. The author questions, "If the technology fails and someone is injured who is at fault-the driver or the manufacturer?" This question is an excellent example of the negative possibilities that could occur with "smart cars." If a driver's vehicle fails to accomplish its task, not only does the driver suffer damage, but another individual in their car also will. This incident should definitely be blamed on the manufacturer, considering the human was supposed to trust their vehicle when they purchased it. These effects will only cause hundreds or thousands of lawsuits for the manufacturers. Finally, the author implies with questioning, "Wouldn't drivers get bored waiting for their turn to drive?" This example not only supports the possibility of the driver falling asleep, but also the encouragement of the use of other technology while driving and becoming quite distraced. For example, if another driver's car happens to malfunction and so happens to begin to collide with another car, the other driver may have been able to avoid the collison if they were not distracted by other technological devices. Although the author states the intentions of manufacturers usung cameras to watch drivers while the car operates, the car cannot force a human to stay focused. Humans tend to rely on technology too much, which will happen with these cars-an accident waiting to happen.

In conclusion, the idea of semi-autonomous vehicles are an aspect of our advanced future that will ultimately ruin the ways of original driving and of course create a lazier world than ever before. Driving test may not even be neccessary since humans will soon not even be operating their own car. So, who says we can't put children behind the wheel of a semi-autonomous vehicle if it is supposedly "driverless?"

This would also lead to less polluting emmisions from cars around the world. With the fact that any automaton takes an artificial intelligence (A.I.) to function, the risk of the A.I. malfunctioning is very dangerous. Similar to how many Toyota cars accelerated and ignored braking mechanisms years ago, a mishap with the cars' programs could cause rampant chaos. Whether this would be pinned on a individual driver in a personal car, the manufacturer, or the man in the driverless car is still asked. The creators of these driverless cars are looking ahead, hoping that these laws become more friendly towards A.I. controlled cars. All the cars that are considered driverless have functions to alert the one behind the wheel to take charge incase of tricky to navigate situations. This makes the law seem a bit ridiculous to outright ban driverless cars from public roads, when they have a return of zero accidents, and have a multitude of safety precautions.

As technology reaches new heights every passing year in the world, it's important to embrace the new ideas that come along. Driverless cars have been worked on for plenty of years, and everyday they're coming closer to the fully realized dream that they began as. Yes, the risk makes the cars seem dangerous, and the law isn't in favor of them, but at the end of they day, the facts are on the side of driverless cars. They have zero reprted accidents, multiple safety precautions, and a real driver in them at all times incase things go south. Driverless cars are going to lead the next chapter of human innovation, and they'll do so on their own.
